en: Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme worship of the Śiva-liṅga,
which bestows all worldly enjoyment and yields the fruit of all gifts and sacrifices.
Worship is said to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
[It may be made] of gold and jewels, or likewise of stone, metal, or wood.
Sadāśiva, endowed with all ritual offerings,
should always be worshipped by the practitioner in a minute mandala, in water, on a cloth, or within his own self.
The worship of an image with Vedic hymns is traditionally taught for one's own benefit;
wherever one performs the sacrifice, there the invocation and dismissal are supreme.
One should worship them with all ritual services;
their invocation is described as being performed in the heart, in the sun, in the gods, in fire, on the earth, and also in water.
One should meditate on Hara within these seven— the wind, the sky,
and the others— and withdraw [the mind] from them.
And when the gods are invoked, [one invokes] Maheśvara, who is all-pervading;
but at the conclusion of the worship, [they depart] by themselves...
(…………………) Therefore, there is no need for purification, ritual sipping, bathing, or the application of ash and rudrākṣa beads specifically regarding the *liṅga*.
Accompanied by the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna), the purification of the self is accomplished;
it includes sweeping, anointing, and being provided with flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
The purification by bathing is proclaimed to be performed with canopies, incense, and lamps;
[one should also provide] a shallow bowl, a water-vortex vessel, a vardhanī pitcher, a conch, and a pearl-oyster shell.
Purification and washing with mantras are proclaimed as the purification of vessels;
all implements, such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, should be infused with fragrance in the waters.
The purification of the substances is proclaimed by means of the ten-syllable [mantra];
having discarded the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings), one should purify the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the *vāruṇa* [mantras].
Purification and washing with the *astra-mantras* are proclaimed as the purification of the *liṅga*.
[The mantras] beginning with [the seed-syllable] *ra* and so forth, or all of them, should be joined with the word "namas" at the end.
Purity of the mantra is proclaimed as follows:
it should be employed during worship through ritual cleanliness, sipping water (ācamana), bathing, the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and the application of sacred ash.

[Having performed] the purification, the beautiful seat (*rucirāsana*), the threefold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the fivefold elemental limbs (*bhūtāṅgabhāva*), the cutting of the body, burning oneself like a withered tree, the immersion in nectar (*amṛtāplāvana*), the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), the placement of the thirty-eight digits (*kalānyāsa*), and having abandoned the natural state (*prākṛtabhāva*) through the contemplation "I am Śiva" (*śivoham-bhāvana*), [one performs] the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*), the purification of the materials (*dravyaśuddhi*), and the worship of the deities of the gateway (*dvāradevārcana*).
Having worshipped the retinue and performed the worship with the Gāyatrī,

[one performs] the dismissal of the *nirmālya*, the purification of the *liṅga*, the purification of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the worship of the support and the supported, the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the placement of all mantras, the invocation (*sannidhāna*), the confinement (*sannirodhana*), and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*).
Welcoming with water for the feet, water for sipping, and water for the guest-offering; consecration with water; garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and decorations;
the waving of lights (*nīrājana*); the display of ashes, the mirror, the parasol, and the fly-whisk; the visualization of the ten mudrās and the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*);
worship, food offerings (*naivedya*), sacrificial oblations (*bali*), and the dismissal of the remains (*nirmālya*); and finally, water for sipping and betel leaf as mouth-perfume.
The festivals consisting of the worship of the book, recitation, meditative absorption, hymns of praise, circumambulation, prostrations, and so forth;
as well as the worship of the sandals, the dismissal of the weapon-mantra, dance, song, instrumental music, and services such as the sprinkling of water from the crest-vessel.
Having abandoned all crookedness and deceit, one should place an arrow at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā on this day;
the stone extracted from there is here called a Bāṇaliṅga.
One should avoid what is visible to the planets and reject it; however, when giving during a sacrifice, that which is visible should be accepted.
Otherwise, there will be the loss of a son; whereas that which is invisible bestows good fortune and produces sons.
One should know that a smooth [surface] has a high value; this is proclaimed as the standard for the price.
One should know that the face is elevated and is to be worshipped by the gods;
one should worship it for the sake of the Self, measuring from two finger-breadths up to five.
On Mount Śaila, the iron [linga] with its pedestal is especially excellent;
the golden, silver, and copper pedestals are considered middling.
Beyond that, at a distance of one *bhūtāṅgula*, the area for the sake of others (*parārtha*) is proclaimed;
there, gems, pearls, corals, lapis lazuli, and crystal [are placed].
Emerald, topaz, and sapphire produced from gems;
gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, and even counterfeit coinage.
Iron, lead, tin,
silver, gold, sand, cow dung, food made of flour, products of the cow, and likewise fruit.
Fresh butter—these seven are declared to be momentary;
one should know them as the "released arrow" (bāṇa) and should worship them especially.
A ruby bestows prosperity; coral is a cause for victory;
lapis lazuli, according to the Ṛṣis, and crystal grant the attainment of sons.
Emerald (marataka) produces enmity; topaz (puṣparāgaka) effects immobilization;
pearl (mauktika) bestows liberation; and the diamond (vajra) increases health.
A blue [stone] serves for the purpose of killing; the fruit of those born of jewels [is as follows]:
gold is known to bestow prosperity, while silver bestows sovereignty.
Copper is for the sake of abundance of sons; bell-metal is a cause of enmity;
brass brings skill; and iron is a cause of decay.
Lead causes disease, while tin increases longevity;
thus has been declared the nature of those derived from minerals. Now hear the effects of the momentary [substances].
Sand brings about liberation; cow dung destroys disease;
food acts as the source of further food; and flour-based offerings bestow nourishment.
Molasses is said to be the state of Śiva, bestowing the fruit of the accomplishment of desired goals;
fresh butter is delightful, and its fruit shall be momentary enjoyment.
It is said that for all [practitioners], the seat (pīṭha) should indeed be the Sayonira;
however, in the case of one who desires the fruits of worship, the fruit belongs to the worshipper himself.
If worship for the sake of others yields fruit for oneself in all cases,
then [the sequence consists of] the seat, the invitation, the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the installation, and likewise the welcome.
The invocation of presence, the rite of cessation, the visualization of the limbs and sub-limbs,
as well as the offering of water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful oblation, and likewise perfumes and flowers.
Then, with incense and lamps, there is the ritual bath, as well as a garment and a sacred thread;
likewise, there is perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the waving of lights (nīrājana).
Ornaments, fans, and so forth, as well as the display of mudrās and the offering of lamps—
these and many other [acts of worship]...
Furthermore, one should perform meditative concentration (*samādhi*), recitation (*japa*), hymns of praise (*stotra*), circumambulation with prostrations (*pradakṣiṇa-namaskāra*),
the offering of water in cupped hands (*culukodaka-pradāna*), and the veneration of the book (*pustakārādhana*).
The mouth [is to be purified] with the *ārjanīya* mantra;
this is the rule for the forty-fold service performed for one's own sake during the worship of the deity.
Those initiated from among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras,
and others who enter [the sacrificial ground] may perform a sacrifice for their own sake, but they must not perform one for the sake of another.
One who is an Ādiśaiva should perform [rites] for his own sake and for the sake of others;
he who is Śiva himself is an Anādiśaiva, while the twice-born Śiva is an Ādiśaiva.
In the beginning, those initiated by the Anādi-Śaiva [tradition] are the Ādi-Śaivas;
they are endowed with the very lineages and domains previously mentioned.
Born from each respective caste, they consist of the essence of both Śakti and Śambhu.
Power is said to be in the form of the female, while the person is called Śambhu.
They declare that Śakti is identical with Śambhu, as is this entire world of moving and non-moving beings;
for the [four] castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa are a continuous succession in due order.
Previously, she was born from the very mouths of Brahmā;
thereafter, having been born as the common intellect (sāmānyacetā), she is so remembered.
Born from the four faces of Brahmā through the creative power of Śiva, they were produced by the Brahman-weapon;
thus they are remembered as Śiva-brāhmaṇas.
Since they are born from the mouth alone, without the creative emission of Śiva, they are called ordinary Brahmins; one should cause them to attain Śiva through initiation.
Because people enter [the path] from this teaching on the propitiation of Śiva,
therefore Brahmins and others who have been initiated by Śiva must abandon the *praveśaka*.
Those who have received the Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) and for whom no other initiation exists—
know that worship which is fit for all gods is fit only for those who have received the Śiva-initiation.
The true essence of knowledge is bestowed and the bondage of the fetters is destroyed;
because both result in the state of perfection, it is called by the term "initiation" (dīkṣā).
Just as copper that has been processed by alchemy does not return again to its state of being copper,
so too the body that has been transformed by knowledge does not return again to the state of a beast.
Thus the initiation is completed, devoid of birth and the like;
by that very means, the person is freed from the state of primordial nature (prakṛti) and becomes empowered.
Having attained the body of Śiva, he is indeed free from birth and death;
he is not defiled by impurities, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Those who were born from the five faces of Brahmā are remembered as the most excellent Brahmins;
those initiated by Śiva are indeed designated as Śivacetas.
In rites such as daily worship, they are fashioned for the sake of others;
those who know the rules understand that all [images] from the initiation ceremony onwards are worthy of worship.
And for others of the four castes, he should worship it solely for his own sake:
the rudrākṣa, the sacred thread, the turban, and the upper garment.
The ash and so forth are proclaimed as the five mudrās of the Śaivas.
Worship for one's own sake is thus to be known; now hear about worship for the sake of others.
Three nadikas before the rising of the dawn,
one should perform the five great sounds (pañcamahāśabda) for three pādas [of the day] in order to ward off misfortune.
Bell-metal, bronze, skin, gourd, and likewise a hollow tube—
these five great sounds one should offer to Śiva.
It is taught that among the transformations of the great elements, sound is composed of these five.
Dāruka is born from the earth; that branch is called the bow.
That which is born from fire is made of iron; that born from wind is of excellent bamboo;
that which is to be sung is born from space; therefore, it is the transformation of the elements.
The wooden (dāruka), the bamboo (cūka), the conch (śaṅkha),
and the hollow metal (lohaja) are known as the fivefold sounds when combined with all that is to be sung.
Starting from that very moment, one should commence the rite of worship:
namely, purification, sipping water, bathing, and the ritual attendance upon the twilight devotions.
Following this, there is the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) conjoined with libation (tarpaṇa),
as well as the purifying seat (pavitram āsana) and likewise the triad beginning with exhalation (recaka).

The mandala of the principles (tattvas), their colors, their presiding deities, and the syllables of their utterance; thereafter, the piercing of the knots and the origin of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then one should perform the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and thereafter the placement of the digits (kalānyāsa).
Following that, one should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), the purification of the site (sthānaśuddhi), and the ritual with the conch (śaṅkhaka).
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, and the characteristics of the fragrance—
at the time of the arghya, while it is cool and pleasant, one should likewise meditate upon the deity.
One should employ the three fragrances, the eight flowers, and the seven *vāruṇī* [liquors];
all the secondary services (*upacāra*), the sounding of the great bell,
and what is known as the "division of the subjects" (*prajābheda*) follow after the purification of the ritual materials.
The ritual procedure for the worship of the doors, as well as the supreme adoration of the retinue.
Then follows the entry into the inner sanctum (garbhageha), the striking of the great bell,
the removal of the curtain, the cutting [of the cord], and thereafter the purification of the linga.
The purification of the seat, the purification of the site, the face, the feet, and the back;
the seat, the invocation, and the mudrā—this is according to the Kālamata.
The bathing water, the time for bathing, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) consisting of cow-products,
pure water, fragrance, clothing, and likewise ornaments.
The fivefold offering (pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā), their colors and forms,
the ritual of waving lights (nīrājana), and the entire sequence of worship.
Their origin, their description, the offering of food and worship along with its characteristics,
the presentation of oblations, the fire-ritual, and likewise the bali-offering to the retinue.
Next is the procedure for the perpetual festival (nityotsava), followed by the supreme worship of the sandals (pādukārcana),
the Duratokta, the Mādi, the Nitāṇḍava, and the Geyaka.
The offering of water from the hollowed palms, circumambulation, prostration,
the characteristics of the musical instrument, and the sequential procedure for recitation and hymns of praise.
What has been begun according to a particular tantra should be completed according to that same tantra;
what is not mentioned [in one] should be taken from another, having understood it, and one should adopt those [elements] appropriate for it.
O twice-born Śiva, at the time of dawn, Śiva remembered Daṇḍapāṇi:
"O Brāhmaṇa, what is to be done in the north or in the eastern direction?"
Near a village, in a large field, by a pond, beside a well,
on an anthill, at a river, at the root of Darbha grass, or on a great highway.
In a cow-pen, on the bank of a river, in a cremation ground,
at a crossroads, near a temple, or near a sacred tree.
At the foot of a tree where flowers grow, upon a stone, on a mountain, as well as on grass,
a cow, a Brahmin, or a linga, and before the newly risen moon or sun.
One should not void excrement or urine while under the influence of a planet or during a rite for subjugation;
rather, having risen and gone outside the village, one should perform purification.
A wise person should place the sacred thread over the right shoulder at the root of the ear;
having positioned the sun to his right, he should then discharge feces and urine.
Facing south at night, having taken a blade of grass upon the ground,
or else with his head wrapped, he should face in such a way that the wind blows toward him.
Having blocked the nostrils with the hand using the right thumb,
one should perform the *ācamana* rite three times until the mouth becomes pure.
Having taken hold of the penis with the left hand and a lump of earth in the right hand,
one should go to the water's edge and thereafter perform the purification.
A wise man, taking earth the size of an axle-hole with his left hand and water with his right, should wash [himself].
A wise person should indeed purify three things— the penis, the feet, and the hands—
performing purification to such an extent as is necessary for the satisfaction of the mind.
Thus has the rule for householders been stated; that for students is twofold, and now that for forest-dwellers and ascetics is declared to be threefold.
Thus has purity been fully described; now hear concerning the tooth-stick:
[it should be made] from the Plakṣa, bamboo, Nimba, Karanja, Jīvaka, or Kula trees.
One should take a straight, pure, and unknotted branch from a milk-exuding tree, an Apāmārga, or especially a mango tree, cutting it at all its bark-joints.
Having prepared a mouthful of water twelve finger-breadths long and with a circumference equal to the little finger,
one should perform the ritual bath.
The cleansing of the staff has already been described; now the sipping of water (ācamana) is stated twice:
"Let him place his right foot [on the ground] while the left foot remains in the water."
Placing his hands between his knees and shaping them like a cow’s ear,
the wise man should take water in which a grain of black gram has been submerged and drink three mouthfuls without fault.
One should wipe the mouth twice there, gently wiping the face once;
then, having sprinkled water on the feet up to the head, one should not use the thumb and ring finger.
Having touched the right eye and so forth with the index finger and the thumb, but not with the ring finger;
having touched both nostrils with the little finger and the thumb, but not with the middle finger;
and having touched the two ears with the thumb while holding water, but not with the arm.
The navel [is touched] by the thumb alone, while all the tips of the fingers are joined together.
Having touched the region of the heart with the tips of all the fingers and then the head,
the satisfaction of the three Vedas— Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma— is desired.
From wiping the mouth comes pleasure for Atharvaveda and Hāsya;
from constant wiping, the face becomes dear to Gaṇeśa.
By merely sprinkling water on his sides, he would please the sages;
by the mere touch of his eyes, he would please the sun and the moon.
By touching the nose alone, the Aśvins shall become pleased;
and by touching the ears alone, it shall bring delight to the quarters of space.
By touching the arms, the navel, and the heart of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Anila,
as well as the head, it shall become a means of pleasing Śiva.
In the event of hunger or when phlegm has arisen, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the left hand;
then, having touched the ear, wipe the mouth with the thumb.
Having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) in this manner, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
Having thus performed the sipping according to the rule, now hear the procedure for bathing.
A bamboo staff, a purifying brush, a new cloth, a water-pot,
a lump of clay, cow dung, flowers, sesame seeds, myrobalan fruit, and *kuśa* grass.
Having taken turmeric, one should go to a river that flows to the ocean;
if such a river is not available, then to a large lake.
If that is unavailable, there should be a lake; if that is unavailable, a pond;
if that is unavailable, there should be a well; having gone there, one should perform the ritual bath.
A tank is ten times more meritorious than a well, a river ten times more than a tank,
and a river flowing to the ocean is ten times more meritorious than a river for the purpose of bathing.
One should not perform a bath in a well; it should be performed in rivers and the like.
Of these, the ocean is the best, while tanks and similar bodies of water are middling.
Thus, bathing in ponds, wells, and the like is considered the lowest form of bathing;
however, if one faces either the east or the north while bathing, the merit becomes tenfold.
Whether the water be pure or impure, if it is near a temple of Śiva,
it becomes the sacred ford known as Śivagaṅgā by being sprinkled from the waters of Śiva’s abode.
In whatever well or pond the shadow of the limbs of a temple is seen,
the water therein is equal to the Ganges.
Having approached those sacred fords (tīrthas) and performed a bath there especially,
one should sit in a pure place, facing either east or north in due order.
This is declared to be the bath for removing impurities, performed by rubbing the body and its limbs with powders of cow-dung and *āmalaka* fruit; now hear this ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).
[It involves using] fish, frogs, snakes, and other aquatic creatures.
Since they are born even in water at all times, one should not perform purification by means of water.
To destroy that defect, one should prepare a Śiva-tīrtha,
a square measuring one cubit in size, as an ornamented site.
The preceptor, having taken up the clay while uttering the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
should divide it into three parts— either in the east, the south, or the north.

Having recited the Astra-Brahmaśiva mantra, one should place [the water] in the eastern direction and so forth; having consecrated it with the Astra mantra, one should cast it below those two [into the pit], and then cast it into the center of the sacred bathing site (tīrtha) within the ten directions.
One should touch the head, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the feet in their respective order, and then touch all the limbs sequentially with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra.
One should bathe with royal honors and with *āmalaka* and other substances during the night;
one should perform the ritual attendance upon the twilight (*sandhyopasthāna*) according to the method instructed by the guru.
Having recited the six-limbed Brahma-mantras, he should internalize the sacred waters within himself;
then, having emerged from the water, he should discard that garment and put on his original clothes.
Bathing at night is not recommended, except during an eclipse of the moon;
[otherwise], it causes the son's blood to flow constantly, as if produced by the night itself.

Therefore, one should not perform bathing or drinking [in such circumstances]; nor should one touch gold or water, except by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). At evening, at sunrise, during the act of shaving, and during sexual intercourse—
Bathing is prescribed as the sixth [purifier] for an evil dream and for contact with a wicked person.
One should especially perform the libation according to the prescribed rite,
specifically for the gods, the sages, and all the ancestors, [beginning with] Vāma, Aghora, and Sadyojāta.
A wise man should offer libations to the gods through the *daivika* tīrtha;
he should satisfy the sages through the *ārṣeya* tīrtha.
A wise man should satisfy the ancestors with the *tīrtha* belonging to the fathers;
the *tīrtha* of the gods is said to be at the base of the little finger.
The *ārṣa* [tīrtha] is at the tips of the fingers; the *paitṛka* is at the base of the thumb;
and the *śivatīrtha* is said to be in the middle of the palm.
The Vaiṣṇava [tīrtha] is on its left, while the Brāhma is said to be on the right;
Sūryatīrtha is to its east, and Vāruṇa is to the west.
In the southeast is the Agni-tīrtha; in the southwest, the Āsura-tīrtha, which consists of two [parts];
in the northwest is the Vāyu-tīrtha; and in the northeast is the Īśāna-tīrtha.
There are twelve sacred sites (*tīrtha*) situated on the right hand of the Brahmins;
therefore, one should with every effort [perform rites] upon the hand of a Brāhmaṇa.
(…………………) there shall be the destruction of all evil. Then, having offered flowers, one should satisfy the deities with the middle of the little finger.
Having thus gratified the sage with water from his two hands using the tips of his fingers and with kuśa grass,
he performed the rite of sacrifice by pouring water mixed with sesame seeds in a counter-clockwise direction.
The preceptor should satisfy the ancestors as well, using the root mantra with the right thumb and forefinger,
offering twenty oblations for each individual.
One should satisfy with ancestral waters (paitṛka-udaka) the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather, as well as the maternal grandfather and his paternal ancestors.
With his left hand and both hands, with loose hair, and with sesame seeds,
one should likewise perform bathing, worship of the gods, fire-offerings, and the recitation of mantras.
Silence is prescribed during the six acts that must necessarily be performed while eating;
the rite of libation (tarpaṇa) has been fully described—now hear the rule for the purifier.
Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water, the wise man should perform every ritual act with a pavitra-grass ring upon his hand.
Kuśa, kāśa, uśīra, dūrvā,
pīhika, viśvāmitra, and yava— these are proclaimed as the seven types of darbha grass.
If the base is thick, it is a woman; if the tip is thick, it is a neuter. When the base and the tip are equal, such is the characteristic of a male blade of *darbha* grass.
One should perform the purification immediately with a *gopāla* (cow-hair brush), *kuśa* grass, *darbha* grass, or a mountain of golden luster,
using four or five folds [of cloth].
One should know that a purifier made of three blades of darbha grass brings peace;
one made of five brings prosperity, and one made of four is for malevolent rites.

For rites for the gods, there should be two darbha blades; for rites for the ancestors, how many should there be? There should be a space of four finger-breadths in the middle, and the knot should be one finger-breadth.
The characteristic of the pavitra is that it should be two finger-breadths wide;
one should perform the rite of sipping water (ācamana) with the pavitra held in hand.
The sacred thread (pavitra) must not be defiled by food remnants; one should avoid using what has been soiled by eating.
Its tip has Rudra as its deity, and likewise, its knot has Viṣṇu.

The bracelet has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the sacred thread (pavitra) has the deities of the sacrificial grass as its presiding deity; just as the thunderbolt belongs to Indra and the trident to Hara.
Just as the discus of Viṣṇu is the purifier for a Brāhmaṇa,
one should likewise apply it to both hands, specifically upon the ring fingers.

A pair of staffs made of three hundred and sixteen finger-breadths each, sacrificial grass with its tips pointing outward, an incomparable banner-pole with a tuft of hair resting at its head, a hundred blades of *sāgraja* grass,
a water-pot, five types of flowers, a spread of grass, a snake, and a *hvivāva*— these nine [are required].
One should recite ten, three, six, one, and one [times] for the [mantra] called Jñāna, and once for the Grāhika.

The sacrificial ladle (sruk) should be thick, resembling a snake's hood, straight, dark-colored, and placed on the left; it should be whetted even by an insect, sharp, auspicious, and provided with a handle.
Likewise, one should prepare the enclosure for the pit (kuṇḍa-veṣṭi) and the enclosing sticks (paridhi) intended for the fire-oblation (homa).
The sacrificial grass was well-straightened, the fuel-sticks were of the proper measure, and the staff was held at its tip as prescribed.
The characteristics of the purifier have been declared; now hear the procedure for the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna). Cow dung from a tawny cow is excellent, while that from a white cow is middling.
The inferior [type] is said to be red-black; it should be taken on a lotus leaf by the Grāhaka.
One should take the cow-dung with the Sadyojāta mantra and form the ball with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The most excellent practitioner from another region should perform purification with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
one should burn [the impurity] with the Śiva-mantra and cause it to be grasped by means of the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
The wise man should place it in a gourd vessel or cast it into ashes;
or, having placed it in a new earthen jar, he should protect it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should recite the Pañcabrahma mantras along with the Śivāṅgas and the Vyomavyāpin mantra once;
then, with the right hand alone, one should place [the water] upon the left hand.
One should smear the head with the Īśāna mantra, the face with the Tatpuruṣa, the heart with the Aghora, and the arms, thighs, and navel with the same. Then,
one should smear the back and the chest with the Bahurūpa mantra.
One should apply the Tripuṇḍra using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the forefinger.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the Tripuṇḍra;
through its three lines, it represents creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Whether during the forenoon meal, while seated, or even upon a bed,
the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with ashes provides protection from all dangers.
The daily bath with sacred ash brings prosperity, purity, and liberation; it is meritorious and brings the world under one's influence day after day.
(…….. Keśava [is established] in the two arms, Īśvara-prīti in the heart, and Prajāpati in the navel.
Durgā and Sarasvatī are likewise on the shoulders and the back;
the two Aśvins are on the knees, and Pañcaga is on the feet.
Whatever merit is gained from bathing in all sacred fords, and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacred fords,
that is accomplished by bathing in ashes multiplied ten million times ten million.
For all members of the four castes— whether woman, man, or eunuch—
one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) three times a day, twice a day, or once a day.
One who provides protection for all shall go to the world of Śiva.
One should apply the smearing of ashes in the presence of Śiva, on the path, in the presence of the gods, the fire, or the guru,
and likewise on pure ground.
Having bowed down to those substances and likewise to the one from whom they were received, a person should then scatter the sacred ash;
for as many atoms of that ash as fall upon the ground, [so many merits shall he obtain].
For as many thousands of ages as there are grains of ash that one has swept from the ground with the hand when it has fallen through negligence, the doer of that act shall go to hell.
Having touched [the ground] with the head and the chest,
a space of six finger-breadths in width is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for Kṣatriyas is four finger-breadths in width;
that for Vaiśyas is three finger-breadths, which grants all desires.
For Śūdras and for women, it should be one finger-breadth;
likewise for those associated with each of these, the wise man shall achieve the destruction of all sins.
Seeing a bad dream, touching a wicked person,
or being unable to bathe— these always apply to sick men.
By bathing with ashes they become pure and indeed fit for worship;
may the fevers, piśācas, and the afflictions that come upon the sick depart.
The Kumāragrahas, Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and even the Ḍākinīs;
the Brahmarākṣasas, Udgīṣas, Bhūtakīṣṭhakas, and Gulmakas.
All the internal cavities [contain] eighty diseases of wind (vāta),
sixty-four of bile (pitta), and seventy-five of phlegm (kapha).
O tiger, for all fears, all protective rites are performed;
likewise, the bilva fruit in the form of a liṅga and bamboo leaves are used.
One should cause the Udumbara tree to be planted at the Aśvattha tree according to the instruction of Śambhu;
likewise, for the destruction of one's own misfortune, during meals, and when bathing in water.
Upon touching a eunuch or a Śūdra woman, one should perform the Āgneya bath;
furthermore, one should apply a circular Puṇḍra beginning with thirty finger-breadths.
The trident, the crescent moon, the lamp, and the fivefold sequence;
the circular mark on the upward-facing [forehead] and the triple-tilaka as prescribed before.
O Six-faced One, a trident is declared for the right face, a half-moon for the western,
and the form of a lamp for the northern face.
Having slept, eaten, drunk water, or performed necessary duties such as answering the call of nature,
one should perform an ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) while wearing wet clothes.
Likewise, when touched by others such as crows,
dogs, or those of inferior castes, as well as by village pigs or cocks, it becomes as impure as a cremation ground.

One should perform the Vāruṇa bath together with those who consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya-bhojaka), ghosts (preta), those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), the fallen (apatita), and likewise with those who follow other heretical paths.
Even after performing a hundred ablutions in water and a thousand ritual baths with mantras,
one becomes equal to Rudra merely by smearing oneself with sacred ash.
Just as evil deeds are destroyed when one protects oneself in all directions,
therefore it is called "rakṣā" (protection), for it bestows the hand of Śiva. It is prosperity that brings prosperity to men, and protection that provides protection to many.
It is called *bhasita* because it is spoken (*bhāsanāt*), and it is called *bhasma* because it consumes impurities (*kalmaṣabhakṣaṇāt*).
When the fire has entered into that very ash which was its support,
one who is radiant through the ash-bath appears like the fire itself.
A learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) even in his mind;
for it is ordained that upon hearing [of its violation], he becomes an outcaste fallen from his sacrificial fire.
Those women who desire the form of men after they have applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) bring about their own destruction,
as if by drinking poison, even while seeking eternal life.
The initiation by the river, the penance, the mantra-practitioner, the one who knows the yantras, and the deities— these [are the means],
along with the names of the vidyās, excluding the greatness of the sacred ash.
Neither that bath, nor that meditation, nor that knowledge,
nor its fruit belongs to the Brahmin who has performed it without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on his body.
Truthfulness, purity, recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and other deities—
all this merit is in vain for one who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra.

Having committed the drinking of liquor, the killing of a Brahmin, or adultery with another's wife, one should lie on ashes; for one who lies on a bed, the meditation on Rudra is prescribed as the expiation.

One is liberated from all sins; this ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) constantly and perpetually effects purification, destroys disease, grants excellent liberation, is equal to the holy ford of the Gaṅgā, removes poison, destroys anger, and brings perfect peace.

O Lord of Pārvatī, [grant] the grace that subdues Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas, which brings about powerful destruction, complete satisfaction and nourishment, and the subjugation of all people in the world for the happiness of every person.
The ash-bath is the supreme sacred site, the constant destroyer of sins;
the ash is Śiva himself in visible form, and the ash is the ruler of the three worlds.

He who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, for the sake of the supreme goal, and for purification— [attains these benefits].
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
this is declared to be the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), which is called the bath of Mahendra.
Standing in the present moment with purity,
facing eastward, with arms not raised, and with the left hand placed upon the right.
One should recite the root mantra with words purified by the breath;
thereafter, the wise person should offer salutations to the face of the Sun and others.
When this is done, one is liberated from great sins; of this there is no doubt.
The bath known as Māhendra has been described; now hear about the Māruta.
O Lord of the Earth, it should be performed either in the forenoon or in the afternoon, but never during the period of menses.
Then, having been consecrated, the mantra-practitioner, recollecting the root mantra,
performs the mantra-bath at the end of that, after washing his hands and feet.

Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he then pours water into the vessel with the "all-pervading space" (vyomavyāpin) mantras, the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) mantras, and the five Brahmans.
Consecrate that water once with the root mantra alone;
then, using that empowered water, [protect yourself] with the root mantra and the armor mantra.
Likewise, touching [the body] three times from the crown of the head down to the feet causes the destruction of all diseases, provided that the destruction of all sins has been accomplished.
The bath known as Vāruṇa, Māhendra, and Māruta, along with that designated as Mantra—
this fivefold bath is honored in all ritual undertakings.
The fivefold bath has been fully described; now hear the procedure for the water for the feet and the other offerings:
saffron, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, uśīra root, and likewise white mustard seeds.
Water combined with these alone is called the most excellent *pādya*:
*uśīra*, sandalwood, *dūrvā* grass, and white mustard seeds.
That which is mixed with water alone is called the middling *pādya*;
that which has the appearance of being mixed with sandalwood and *uśīra* is called the lowest *pādya*.
The retention of each [ingredient] individually is best; half of that is considered middling;
half of that again should be known as inferior—this is remembered as the measure for the substances used for the foot-water (pādya).
The water for the feet (pādya) is offered once for each foot, beginning with the right foot; this is known as the substance for the pādya. Now hear about the substance for the ācamana.
Uśīra, nutmeg, camphor, tuṭi, kuṣṭha, and cloves—
these should be used with water to prepare the supreme *ācamanīya*.
Cardamom, cloves, camphor, and uśīra grass combined with jasmine,
when mixed with water, is known as the middle sipping (madhyamācamana).
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) for the youngest [deity] should be mixed with the ashes of cardamom and *elālavaṅga*;
one should determine the proportions of these as previously described.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the mouths; one should maintain an uninterrupted stream of water.
This is declared to be the substance for sipping; now hear concerning the substances for the arghya offering.
(…) *masnā*, fresh butter, the tip of a *kuśa* blade, white mustard seed,
camphor, *laghupatra*, and *lavaṅga* is said to be the eighth.
At the time of worship, one should place upon the head that which is known as *arghya*—
namely, water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, along with unbroken rice and barley grains.
An offering (arghya) consisting of sesame and white mustard seeds is said to be the most excellent;
one made with barley, mustard, rice, and so forth, along with grains of rice, is middling.
Water, rice, and śali grain constitute the lowest grade of the *arghya* offering;
however, one should determine the quantity of the *arghya* substances as previously prescribed.
This is known as the *arghya* substance; now hear [the description] of the bathing substances (*snānadravya*).
With elā, śīra, the three fruits (phalatraya), āmalaka, sugar, camphor, and excellent saffron;
Combined with auspicious *karṇāgara* leaves and fragrant flowers, along with *cūpa*,
*omarjana*, and *maṇipraṇabha*, it should be offered to Śambhu according to what is available.
When the qualities of the aforementioned substances have been obtained in abundance, they should be used by both the wealthy and the poor;
however, bathing with eight *droṇas* of water is declared to be the minimum requirement.
The middling [penance] should be known as double that, and the highest should be triple;
having taken a water-vat, one should fill it with water filtered through a cloth.
Having added one niṣka each of sandalwood, saffron, camphor, tagara, and uśīra,
one should stir them carefully into water.
Having prepared it according to the prescribed rite, one should cause it to be stored securely;
this is to be known as "Auspicious Water" (śivāmbhas), consecrated by the Śiva-mantra.
Now listen to the description of the fragrant substances known as the bathing ingredients:
camphor, saffron, tamāla leaves, khaṭga, and the three fruits.
Sandalwood, uśīra, and iron are said to produce the highest fragrance;
likewise, uśīra, sandalwood, camphor, and the three fruits [are used].
That which is composed of nine types of incense is called the middle-grade fragrance;
camphor, combined with snow and thick [incense], is called the lowest-grade fragrance.
The best substance as a reward is [the full amount]; half of that would be middling;
and half of that (or less) should be known as inferior—thus is the fragrant substance proclaimed.
That which is known as fragrant substance is said to be the characteristic of clothing—
various beautiful garments that are substantial and [durable].
Incensed, excellent flowers, fresh and fragrant, are declared the highest part of the deity; linen is said to be the middling.
A cloth made of cotton threads is considered inferior;
that which measures seven cubits is superior, and six cubits would be middling.

The lowest [quality] cloth should be five cubits; this is declared to be the characteristic of cloth. Black cloth brings about total destruction, and one who wears it incurs the fault of being slain by the king.
One may witness the destruction of a village or the ill-omened ruin of a kingdom,
as far as the measurement of garments and the knowledge thereof is prescribed.
For that many thousands of yugas he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
such is the characteristic of the cloth, and now the characteristic of the conch is being described.

Gold, silver, copper, and especially a vessel of bell-metal—these are the materials; however, a vessel made of *palāśa* or lotus leaves is equal in merit to one of copper. A conch shell is to be known as being of four kinds, corresponding respectively to the Brāhmaṇa and the other castes.
It has a small, elongated, and beautiful form, with the tip and the back being equal in length.
A Brahmin who has filled his belly is called a śaṅkha;
he is foremost, tall, symmetrical, beautiful, and radiant as gold.
A conch that turns to the right is said to belong to a Kṣatriya;
it is slightly yellow in color and possesses a counter-clockwise whorl.
That which is equal in weight to a guru and a laghu is remembered as the Vaiśya-śaṅkha;
that born of a Śūdra is light, long-tailed, and short-backed.
Relying on the slightly dark [portion], it is remembered as the Śūdra-conch;
however, in the midst of the confluence of the Gaṅgā, there are the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya conchs.
Between the Narmadā and the Sindhu, for a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, one should give a conch shell that is completely full;
this is called the Dakṣiṇāvarta.
The front of the belly is said to consist of Kuhu; the belly is proclaimed to be Gaṅgā. On the back is said to be Brahmā, and on the sides are the two deities Śāśvata and Aśvinī.
The preceptor, being a god, a sage, and a seer, should hold the conch while recollecting the Śakti-mantra and the Sāvitrī verse of the Aṅgiras lineage.

The characteristic of the conch should be thus; now hear the doctrine of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). Having duly established the mantra at the aperture of the head according to the ritual for the extraction of milk, one should perform worship.
One should offer curd to Indra, fresh ghee to the son of the Sun (Yama), honey-mixed [ghee] to Soma,
sugar-candy to Varuṇa as prescribed by the ancients, and likewise the dhātrī fruit to Agni.
(…) O Śambhu, one should perform the night-rite when the wind is favorable, using kuśa grass and water;
likewise, one should draw four lines with their tips pointing eastward and likewise with their tips pointing southward.
The supreme preceptor should have [the vessels] made with a measurement of one palm-span (*tāla*).
For the *śāli* rice, three *prasthas* is best; two *prasthas* would be middling;
and two *prasthas* is declared to be the lowest for each of the jars individually.
It should be adorned with half that amount of rice, and also with half of that amount of sesame seeds.
With parched grain, flowers, and Darbha grass, and especially with sugar,
they filled jars endowed with auspicious marks up to four prasthas.
One should wrap all the spaces resembling windows with thread;
the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) has Brahmā as its deity, and the darbha grass has Viṣṇu as its deity.
The Sūtra has Īśvara as its presiding deity; the Adhidevas are proclaimed [as follows]:
milk, curd, ghee, and honey combined with sugar.
One should worship the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five Brahmans according to the thread and the mantra:
honey, milk, ghee, clarified butter, and the essence of sugarcane, each separately.
This is declared to be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); one should worship the limbs of Brahmā, with each [substance] measuring a full prastha, while the middling measure is half of that.
Half of that is to be known as the lowest; here, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are spoken of.
These five nectars are for the individual consecrations (abhiṣeka).
The consecration should be performed with the five Brahmans, beginning with Sadyojāta;
[the practitioner] is glorified in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of kalpas.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with curd, milk, and ghee,
as well as with coconut water, honey, and the five products of the cow (brahmapañcaka).
This is declared to be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); now hear [the description] of the five fruits:
the plantain, the jackfruit, and likewise the coconut fruit.
The mango and the citron—these constitute the five fruits.
One should perform the consecration separately for each, starting from the east (Sadyojāta) up to the northeast (Īśāna).
One should place milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar-cane juice,
as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five parts of the five trees (pañcāṅga), each in its proper order.
The six products of the cow— cow dung, bile, urine, milk, curd, and ghee—
are pure and all are bestowers of success.
In the middle of the nine squares, milk should be placed for Indra;

curds in the direction of Yama; ghee for Indra in the western (Vāruṇa) direction; two pieces of cow dung in the southeast (Agni), southwest (Nirṛti), northwest (Vāyu), and northeast (Īśāna) corners; and flour—
Then, one should crush that with a mallet.

One should know that Śiva and Sadāśiva are the *puruṣatattva* designated as Kāla; [they are] established in the heart, perfectly tranquil, and of the nature of splendor, [manifesting] as water from jewels, nectar, and the clarified butter in vessels, as well as milk, curd, ghee, cow-urine, kuśa-water, and red chalk for the feet.
A wise man should not frequent the company of those devoted to destiny, the arts, passion, or the assemblies of the learned.
One should employ the vessels with the heart-mantra: "Supratiṣṭham," "Suśāntam," "Tejovat," "Ūtijaṃ," and "Amṛtam. Thus are the vessels joined.
Ghee from a tawny cow is best, milk from a black cow is excellent;
curd from a white cow should be considered foremost, as indeed is the urine of a red cow.
Even if it resembles a skull-bowl, that which is spoken but once is divine;
thus indeed is the acquisition of a cow, whether it be white or black.
At the proper time and place, with a serene mind, one should take auspicious cow-dung from a cow together with her calf—
dung that is found on the ground, not fallen, and situated in the air.
Regarding food, one should diligently take milk that has been freshly drawn,
as well as thick curds that are very firm and pleasing to the sight.
Clarified butter is for Kāśyapa, curd is said to be for Kauśika;
milk belongs to Bhāradvāja, and likewise cow dung to Gautama.
Agastya and cow’s urine are proclaimed by the sages as having Agastya for their deity;
ghee has Rudra as its deity, and curd has Soma as its deity.
Milk has Śukra as its presiding deity, and cow dung has Arka;
cow urine is in the Gaṅgā, and these are the presiding deities of the five products of the cow.
The best [quantity] is thus a droṇa; the middling is half of that;
the lowest should be known as half of that again—one should thus determine the three types.
One prastha of ghee, two prasthas of curd,
three prasthas of milk, and four prasthas of cow dung.
Six *prasthas* of cow urine are praised as the best;
half a *prastha* of ghee and one *prastha* of curd are likewise prescribed.
One prastha of milk and one prastha of cow dung, two prasthas of cow dung,
and three prasthas of cow urine constitute the medium-sized [preparation], which is highly recommended.
One *kuḍupa* of ghee and two *kuḍupas* of curd;
three *kuḍupas* of milk, and likewise one *prastha* of cow dung.
One *prastha* or half a *prastha* of cow urine is recommended for the lowest [grade];
one should especially worship the deities beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
Water from kusha grass, milk, curd, and ghee— when used one, two, three, four, five, or six times [in the ritual], they respectively ward off enemies, grant sons, and bestow liberation.
Cow dung destroys sin and brings about auspiciousness; cow urine is the water of the stream;
the water from the tips of *kuśa* grass accomplishes everything when mixed with fragrance.
Having smelled [the powder], it bestows delight upon the lives of men; this is the triad of bathing powders for the Victors.
Now hear about the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), known as the Brahmakūrca.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kuśa* grass—this is known as the *brahmakūrca*; one should sprinkle it [upon oneself] at the time of worship.
The wise one should offer water for the feet at each foot, pouring it once upon each;
he should offer water for sipping into the mouths with an unbroken stream of water.
Having placed the *arghya* upon the head, one should apply fragrant unguents as anointment to the limbs;
having placed flowers upon the crown of the head, one should offer incense to the nostrils.
For instance, one should place the lamp in the eyes and the food to be eaten in the palms of the hands;
likewise, the food to be chewed, the soft food, the drink, as well as that which is to be sucked and licked.
One should quickly offer the flower and then give the water for sipping (ācamana);
the water for washing the feet has Earth as its deity, and the water for sipping has Sarasvatī as its deity.
The Arghya has Śrīdevī as its presiding deity; the fragrance has Vāyu as its deity;
the flower has the Gandharvas as its deity; and the incense has Candra as its deity.
The twice-born man should contemplate the lamp as having Vāka as its deity for all [the offerings];
and he should hold it with his left hand for all the deities of the sacrifice.
The water for the feet (*pādya*) destroys sin; the water for sipping (*ācamana*) brings about prosperity;
the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) ensures the success of one's actions; and the fragrant paste (*gandha*) becomes like Mount Govardhana.
Flowers are said to bestow nourishment, and the offering of incense (*dhūpa*) grants purification.
The lamp is said to bring subjugation, while the ārātrika bestows victory.
Ash is for the protection of the universe, and especially for those who rule the earth;
the libation is said to bestow knowledge, and the parasol is the preservation of one's command.
The yak-tail whisk (chāmara) brings about the destruction of enemies; song and instrumental music bestow happiness;
the food offering (naivedya) results in the increase of grain; and the water offering (pānīya) provides protection for one's life.
For the sake of rain, one should perform propitiatory rites for the planets using milk and other sweet substances;
likewise, the offering of betel and flowers brings happiness to the people.
Bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is declared to destroy disease and remove impurity;
the gift of clothing here is said to bring about self-renewal.
By performing worship with the limbs of enjoyment, one shall obtain all enjoyments;
by [worshipping] the king and the kingdom, one shall obtain great enjoyment for all.
Gold, gems, coral, and other such things, as well as ornaments that bring about wealth,
the fruit of abundant crops, and the destruction of all evil deeds— [all these result from it].
And for all weapons such as the trident, it shall consist of the essence of all mantras;
it serves to destroy disease, grief, and enemies, and it is the destroyer of all poverty.
It brings about the destruction of all enemies, the eradication of all calamities,
and bestows peace upon all men, and especially upon the gods.
The rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) for that [deity] are said to consist of twelve measures (mātrā);
the water for the feet (pādya) should consist of five measures, and the water for sipping (ācamana) should consist of three measures.
The arghya offering should be one mātrā; the incense is said to be six mātrās;
the lamp is said to be six mātrās; and the incense (dhūpa) should be fifteen mātrās.
The worship with the *ārātrī* lamp is the seventh, while the *nīrājana* rite is the sixteenth;
thereafter, one should cause the ashes to be distributed, which is said to be the seventeenth.
The fan should be three mātras in length, the chowrie ten mātras,
the parasol five mātras, and the libation for the sages one mātra.
Then one should perform the offering (nivedana) consisting of twenty-four measures;
the time for the presentation of the bali-offering is twenty-five measures more than that.
The number of nāḍikās for the sake of bliss is said to be three hundred;
having understood this through the relationship of the worshiper and the object of worship, one should begin the sacrifice.
The one to be worshipped is Śiva himself, and the worshipper is said to be Śakti.
If the worship is deficient, disease shall arise; if it is devoid of flowers, there will be the destruction of the lineage.
If it is devoid of fragrance, one suffers from leprosy; if devoid of water, it brings suffering;
if devoid of incense, happiness is destroyed; and if devoid of a lamp, there is loss of wealth.
If the food offering (naivedya) is omitted, there will be famine; if the mantra is omitted, poverty;
if the clothing is omitted, a great disease; and if the fire-oblation (homa) is omitted, a loss of strength.
If the bali offering is deficient, there will be a great disease; if the rājan is deficient, death;
and if the bilva fruit, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice are deficient, one shall encounter danger from enemies.
If the bell is omitted, deafness results; if the mudrās are omitted, there is fear from the gods;
and if the daily fire-ritual is omitted during worship, it becomes fruitless.
If there is an absence of constant festivals, there will be fear for the king and the kingdom; and if there is an absence of grain and wealth, there will surely be the wrath of the gods.
If the rite is performed without the necessary materials, or likewise without the mantra,
or with a deficiency in the worship of the Guru, there will be failure and the destruction of one's sons, wife, and land.
If the sound of musical instruments is neglected, one is humiliated by the Rākṣasas;
therefore, with every effort and preceded by devotion to the deities, [one should perform it].
The maddala drum brings happiness, while the tāla cymbal removes afflictions;
the paṭaha drum destroys sin, and the bherī drum increases nourishment.
The vāma-sena is indeed dear; the kaṃsa-tāla brings pleasure;
the jhallarī is desired by those who seek enjoyment; and the kumbha-instrument bestows liberation.
The playing of the nāḍī-sandhāna instrument yields the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
likewise, the flute and vocal song increase one's sons and grandsons.
The joining of beautiful shields, the sound of musical instruments that brings victory,
combined with the blast of conchs— this wards off all enemies.

Dancing brings about the destruction of disease, and singing increases longevity; drama results in an increase of grain, and likewise, it is auspicious for one of pure conduct. By means of the Śaṅkhamārga in Koṇḍalī, the king shall obtain victory.
Nyāla brings the three worlds under one's control, while kiṭuka bestows happiness.
For the purification of defects, the Kadruṭī [mudrā] arises from the vision of Murasā;
through the stream [of practice], there shall be the attainment of all perfections, and the mind shall be the subduer of kings.
One should perform the *triyaṣṭa*, the *bhoga-mokṣa*, the *kattṛkā* for subduing women,
the *garbhageha*, and other rites with the Śiva-dvija.
The mere study of the Vedas is the station of the Brahmins within the pavilion;
for those who are initiated and ascetic, their station is in the outer pavilion.
One should circumambulate upon seeing a stūpa in all other types of births.
Thus has the procedure for the water for the feet and so forth been explained; now hear the ritual for the flowers.
It is of four kinds: white, red, yellow, and black.
Furthermore, the white [variety] consists of the *punnāga*, the *śaṅkhapuṣpa*, and the *mallikā*.
The *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *mandāra*, *bahukarṇikā*, *dvikarṇi*, *kurava*, *jāti*, *lakṣmī*, and likewise the *vakula*;
the white *arka*, *mālatī*, *droṇa*, *atasi*, and white *lodhra*.
Vṛṣakā was born with flowers, and likewise [the earth]... ||
One should offer white flowers that are sattvic;
one should worship with whatever flowers are available during the forenoon.
The red lotus, the palāśa, the red water-lily, the pāṭala, the mausalī,
the durdhūra, the bṛhatī, and the karavīraka.
Vyādhrī, ratamandāra, vāṭikā, and likewise vejikā—
these red flowers should be designated as belonging to the rājasa quality.
Śaunakya, Karṇikāra, Campaka, Hemadurdhūra, Āragvadha, Cakoraṇḍa, Śaileya, and Girikarṇikā.
These mixed flowers that are black are indeed characterized by tamas;
therefore, one should designate blue lotuses and the like as being of the nature of tamas.
A flower equal to the blue lotus has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
yet a thousand golden flowers shall indeed become equal to the blue lotus.
One should not discard blue lotuses, golden flowers, or faded garlands;
rather, having purified them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should commence worship once again.
One should cause the *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, white *arka*, white *padmaka*,
blue lotus (*utpala*), *pāṭalī*, and *droṇa* to be offered at midday;
as well as the *campaka*, *bejikā*, *bhadrī*, *dhurdhūra*, and *bahukarṇika*.
Mālatī and Mallikā, indeed, should be offered at the onset of night.
One should cause the *jātī*, the blue lotus, the *bilva* leaf, the *kadambaka*, the *dvikarṇī*, and the *bhadrā* to be offered during the half-watch of the night.
The bowl-leaf tree, the ascetic’s plant, along with the abhadra and tātakī,
apāmārga, kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, the five bilva fruits, and likewise the śamī tree.
Bilva, kapittha, nirguṇḍī, gharaṇa, and likewise śaraṇa—
these five bilvas are the destroyers of great sins.
Tulasīdala-saṃjña, Jambuka, Nāganandikā,
Ekapatrāravinda, and likewise Viṣṇukrānti.
Among all species of leaves, the bilva leaf is preeminent;
among all species of flowers, the karavīra is preeminent.
In the same way, for various species of flowers, the leaf and the flower are prescribed;
for the Śamī and Vyāghāta flowers, the fruit is ten thousand or a million.
One should prescribe a hundred thousand white mandāra flowers as the fruit;
therefore, with every effort, one should offer flowers endowed with fragrance.
The offering of *arghya* thus presented shall yield the fruit of all sacrifices.
One should designate as the highest fruit the flower produced from one's own garden;
that which grows in the forest, one should designate as the middling fruit.
(……………………………) one should predict the result.
One should worship with one flower each month;
one should assign the flowers, beginning with the arka, in order throughout the twelve months.
Arka, bilva, apāmārga, droṇa, utpala, paṅkaja,
vyāghāta, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, śamī, campaka, and pāṭalī.
By avoiding other flowers one by one month after another, one attains the fruit that is the destruction of death; of this there is no doubt.
One who worships in this manner for a year shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
This has been declared as the flower of worship; now hear about the flowers to be avoided.
One should avoid the ketakī, mādhavī, kunda, yūthikā, madayantikā,
śirīṣa, japā, bandhūka, and japā flowers.
Kiṃśuka, ārtakaraja, nīlakaṇṭhī, moca, the flowers of talapa and peṭaka, and the flowers of piśāca;
One should avoid these flowers so that one becomes worthy of worshipping Viṣṇu;
one should offer the Palāśa flower to Brahmā and Tulasī to Keśava.
The flower of the *candravaktrā* plant brings delight to Indra;
one should reverently worship Śiva with all white flowers.
One should discard the black variety, the girikarṇī, and the kiṃśuka;
one should also avoid that which is over-ripe, unripe, or still in bud.
Even flowers pierced by insects or covered with cobwebs,
or those that have fallen of their own accord, should not be gathered for one's own clothing.
One should avoid flowers that are from the previous day, those that are stale,
those brought in a garment, those brought by hand, and those touched by a crow.
The *pratyuṣa* flower is one that blooms at dawn and has withered by night;
it is brought from below the navel and is touched by the feet.
It has been smelled by birds, as well as by dogs, beggars, cocks, and the like;
it has been touched by cats, mice, buffaloes, donkeys, and monkeys.
One should avoid that which is blown upon by breath, touched by those afflicted with disease,
touched by women in their menses and the like, and the cremation ground.
The *varjapuṣpa* has been fully described; now hear the characteristics of incense (*dhūpa*):
honey, sugar, candied sugar, *kunduru*, and saffron.
Indeed, among all fragrances, incense is what brings pleasure to Śiva;
it may consist of one, two, three, or four ingredients, such as conch-shell, sandalwood, and iron.
It was likewise increased in sequence by the addition of *kaiduka*,
and similarly infused with *śītārī* incense and honey.
Sandalwood, nityāsaṃ, kundaruka,
saffron, mekha, black iron, and camphor, in that order.
Having taken seven *ṛṣabhas*, the Vedas, and other portions from the *aśvinī* and *bārā* [constellations],
one should grind them into a powder and soak it thoroughly with honey.
These very things, when burned as incense, shall become a source of delight for Śiva.
[The offering] with four times as much sugar is known as *induriṣka*.
And the incense possessing eight qualities was created by Rudra;
[it consists of] black iron and resin...
(……….. slightly mixed with camphor, this is declared to be the most excellent incense, and it should be thoroughly saturated with honey.
That which is combined with sandalwood and uśīra, mixed with honey,
and prepared in the same manner as previously described for the light [incense], is called the medium incense.
Guggulu mixed with clarified butter is called the lowest incense;
it is combined with lamp-charcoal and held in the left hand by a bell-ringer.
Taking up the incense burner, one should offer incense according to the prescribed rite;
one should cause the incense known as Sāda and the Śiva-incense to be offered to Caṇḍeśa.
Having thoroughly cleansed the incense burner and filled it with fire from wood,
one should offer incense with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra and present it to all [the deities].
The offering is for Sadāśiva, while the incense for the sakala-rite is for Abhicāraka;
having thus described the substances for incense, now hear the characteristics of the lamp.
One should offer a lamp with the ghee of a tawny cow, or with yellow, red, or white ghee;
if ghee is unavailable, one may instead offer a lamp with pure oil.
Ghee from a Kapila cow is the best; that of others is middling;
goat-ghee and likewise pure oil are inferior.
One should cause a lamp made with camphor wick to be offered— successively of *sāttvika*, *tāmasa*, and again *tāmasa* quality— which bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
One should avoid the clarified butter produced from buffalo milk in all ritual activities.
One should consume the meat of goats and buffaloes, but one must completely avoid [the meat of] ghosts (bhūta).
One should avoid using oils produced from trees for the lamp of Śiva;
however, during a festival, it may be performed, provided one avoids lamps made from other [prohibited] sources.
The lamp should be twelve finger-breadths in height for the best [offering];
the lamp for the middling [offering] should be made four finger-breadths [in height].
Taking three finger-breadths, that lamp should be increased;
from three finger-breadths up to one [cubit], the lamps for the Kṣudra [rite] follow in due order.
The circumference of the thumb should be equal to that which has been stated for it;
the ring finger should have the same circumference, and the middle finger should be beautiful.
The circumference of the wick-holder for the lowest [lamp] should be the width of the little finger;
one should have small lamps made with threads of nine, seven, or five [strands].
For the best [quality], three prasthas of clarified butter are prescribed;
for the middling, half a prastha of clarified butter is declared.
Half of that is to be known as the middling [size]; there are three grades, beginning with the superior.
The flame of the lamp-wick, the light—the worship of the lamp—is dear to Śiva.
Whether one or many, it is for the worship of the deity.
(……………………) in accordance with what is seen [in the scriptures]. (Second line:
Worshipping the Lord Śiva, who is the eternal lamp and free from ailment, especially for the sake of King Śiva, his kingdom, and the practitioner.
One should perceive the auspicious lamp of emptiness for the purpose of the fire-oblation;
by this means, the king who dwells in hell shall perish for the sake of the patron.
Misfortune arises for him and even his fortune perishes;
his life-span is destroyed and he becomes afflicted by disease. (Fourth line) I shall declare the remedy for that, which is not to be disclosed, along with its fruit.
Formerly, Māyā heard this from the presence of Paramaiṣṭhin:
"The best of teachers, knowing it to consist of the Jyotirliṅga,
should meditate upon it— the auspicious Devapriya, which increases the kingdom and the region of the king."
At the time of worship with the lamp, the offering of wine and the ritual substances for worship have been fully described; now hear about the three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma).
The lotus, the svastika, the cow-mouthed, and likewise the formidable;
the needle, the one-legged, the cock, and the heroic.
The Bhadrāsana should be at the back, as well as the Kūrma and the Vimala;
then follow the Daṇḍapiṇḍa, the Gokarṇa, and beyond that, the Siṃhāsana.
The Vṛtta, Udghaṭikā, Gajāsya, and Gajakarṇaka—these twenty postures are proclaimed; one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) while seated upon them.
A stable and comfortable posture is prescribed, which is honored in all the Tantras.
The authority and so forth of the blind [or those with impaired vision] is established in the third quarter.
Therefore, with every effort, one should first practice the postures;
O Lord of Yogis, established in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), one should thoroughly practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O Six-faced One, through *dhāraṇā* one attains perfection;
through *prāṇāyāma*, the perfection of austerity, the perfection of yoga, and eternal, supreme *samādhi*.
O Guha, through prāṇāyāma, one indeed obtains the fruit of heaven and liberation;
it yields the fruit of all the gods and the fruit of all sacred fords.
O child, through prāṇāyāma, one shall surely obtain the fruit of worshipping Śiva.
Upon a deer-skin, or kusha grass,
or a plank, he should sit comfortably facing either the east or the north.
Having avoided eating too much or not eating at all, he should remain composed.
In a secluded place, free from disturbances such as biting insects,
one should keep the neck and head straight and touch the teeth with the teeth.
Seated with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one should not look toward the directions;
having performed the purification of the channels within the temple by means of the lamp of mantra.
Having filled [the right], one should fill the left...
[it] should be joined with... (second line).
The wise one, being composed, should fill [the left] as before.
Beginning from the big toe, let the vital breath remain right here.
One should first exhale through the right and the piṅgalā [nāḍī];
then, with the left hand, one should firmly join the thumb and the index finger against the nostril.
Touching with the right hand, one should exhale the air through the left nostril for five *mātrās*.
With the index finger of the left hand, one should seal the left nostril;
then, having drawn the air out through the right nostril, one should exhale it for five *mātrās*.
In this manner, after five, six, seven, six months, or even a year,
one attains purification of the nose, freed from the defects of the knots;
thereafter, O Six-faced One, there should be breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) performed with the *Prāsāda* mantra.
First, the wise one should fill the abdomen with sixteen mātrās;
holding the breath for sixty-four mātrās, one becomes equal to all the gods.
The breath is exhaled upwards with thirty-two *mātrās*;
thus indeed is the *recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka* for the Brahmins.
One should thus practice sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) constantly;
by means of *prāṇāyāma*, O Guha, one indeed attains prosperity when this sign appears.
Thereafter, the conquest of the vital breaths and so forth, the seed-syllable, the phoneme, and the location;
the letter *ya*, which is the life-force of the vital breath, resembling a dark blue cloud.

The letter *ra* is Fire and the *apāna* breath, which illuminates at the rising of the Sun; the *vyāna* breath is said to be the letter *la*, resembling a wheel or a bandhūka flower. The letter *va* is said to be the *udāna* breath and Varuṇa, resembling a conch shell.
The letter *bha* is said to be equanimity; one becomes Śiva, radiant like crystal.
Located from the heart, the navel, the nose, and the ears down to the big toes—
this is declared to be the seat of the vital breath (prāṇa), extending as far as the Brahma-granthi.
The downward-moving wind (apāna), the penis, the thighs, the chest, and the knees; (in the fifth line:
the abdomen, the shanks, the root of the navel, and the surface of the hips.
Vyāna is located in the eyes, the two nostrils, the region of the throat,
the sides, the back, the belly, the thighs, the shanks, and also the ankles;
Udāna resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet, the hands, and the fingers.
It is equal throughout all bodies, extending from the big toe up to the crown of the head;
it abides by way of the channels through seventy-two thousand gates,
and is established in the twenty-eight corners of the pores of the skin.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is one and the same, for the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed one while residing within;
slowly drawing it all back into the filaments of the heart-lotus.
Having filled [the space] as before,
[one should place] the *ka* and *nda* syllables in the cavity of the palate;
in the case of a rite for peace (*śāntika*), [these should be placed] between two bows at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Upon the emergence of the rope and fire, the deity leads [the soul] to the supreme state of Maheśvara and then to the station of Sadāśiva; it is the deity, not the preceptor, who does so. Thereafter, one attains Nirvāṇa through Mṛtyuñjaya, which is free from rebirth.
Thereafter, one should lead [the soul] along the path of emanation into Śiva himself within that very self;
likewise, Sadāśiva is for five *nāḍī*-units, and Maheśa is for five *ghaṭī*-units.
In the *bindu* there are four *ghatikās*, and in the *nāda* there are three;
in the *jyotsnā* there are two *raktis*, and in the *somayoga* it is situated on the bank.
The *raśmi* [is located] at half a *ghaṭikā*; half of that is within the range of the *śakti*.
The *guhā* is situated at half of that in the center of the heart and in the cavity of the palate.
One should indeed perform the *śivāstra* in the heart by means of *prāṇāyāma* within the cave.
Thus, for one year under the guidance of a teacher, [one practices] externally by means of the *prāsāda* mantra.
But the primary [practice] is *prāṇāyāma*:
exhalation (*recaka*) has Brahmā as its deity, and inhalation (*pūraka*) has Viṣṇu as its deity.
The *kumbhaka* has Viṣṇu (or Rudra) as its presiding deity; these are proclaimed to be the deities of the [three breaths].
Thereby one attains victory over death; therefore, one should master the vital air (*vāyu*).
This is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*.
Having assumed a beautiful posture,
one should begin the arrangement of the directions in the ten quarters with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
Earth, water, as well as fire, air, and space itself;
O Six-faced One,
the elements residing within the body are to be purified in five ways, from the feet up to the head, in their proper sequence.
Having placed earth upon the knees, one should place water at the navel;
having placed fire up to the neck, one should place wind in the head.
(Fourth line) Having placed space at the end of the head, one should place the five elements in their proper order.
The locus beginning with earth and ending with space consists of the deities of the phonemes;
it is square and likewise fourfold in its circles, yellow in color,
extending down to the knees, ending with the color of Rudra, and has Brahmā as its presiding deity.
Next, I shall describe the mandala situated one above the other:
the seed-syllable of the waters, likewise white in color and circular in shape.
From the navel upward, the domain of Viṣṇu presided over by Brahmā is established;
above that element of water, it is triangular and red in color, with flames rising from its upper edge.
And extending up to the neck, it is the presiding deity of the Rudras;
it is six-cornered, smoke-colored, and ends with the element of the Bhūtas in the upper region. Īśvara is proclaimed as its presiding deity, and the Vāyu-tattva is celebrated [therein].
They say it is a circular form, like a crystal at the end of the head;
the peaceful god Sadāśiva is celebrated as "Space" (Ākāśa).
Above that Space, at its limit, is the seed-syllable of Power (Śakti), which is the source of speech.
And at its end is the light of Śiva, resembling pure crystal;
in the supreme, subtle Śivatattva, the mantra of light is proclaimed.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti,
and Śivamaya— these are proclaimed as the seven.
The purification of the feet and so forth, extending up to the knees, is fivefold;
the purification of the thighs, extending from the knees to the navel, is fourfold;
and the purification by fire, from the navel upwards to the throat, is indeed threefold.
The purification of the breath is indeed twofold; one should perform it until the throat is filled.
One should cut the five knots by means of the Pāśupata scripture;
and with the Śiva-weapon at the tip of the Suṣumṇā, one should [cut] the space-knot (ākāśagranthi).
The place of Śiva is proclaimed to be joined at the end of the neck of the lute;
twelve finger-breadths above that is [the next stage].
(…………………) one should unite it with the Tatpuruṣa;
thereafter, one should unite that Śiva with Śiva, the supreme cause.
At the tip of the tongue, twelve finger-breadths [above], pure and as stainless as clear crystal,
within the supreme Śiva-tattva— subtle, of the nature of light, and partless—
one should worship with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and the syllable *aṃ*.
By means of the saṃhāra-mudrā and the haṃsa-mantra, one should unite it with the self;
it shall consist of the seed-syllable of air, situated in the center of the circle of air.
One should contemplate oneself as being consumed like dry wood,
within the triangular realm of fire, adorned with garlands of flames.
Just as the Praṇava, situated within the second syllable, is established above;
beginning from the big toe up to the head, one should burn [the body].
The wise one should burn the physical body as if it were a heap of ashes;
having meditated upon it as a heap of ashes, he should consume his own form with his own luster.

O Tārā, [visualize] the moon situated in the center of the square of the [vowel] class, upon a white lotus; there is the yoga-seat facing downwards. Like pure crystal is the syllable A, which arises from the self.
The principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) is the letter A, and the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva) is the letter Ha.
Having flooded the body with nectar,
one should then contemplate Sadāśiva as the cause of the body and subsequently perform the pervasive breath-exercise (*vyāna*) upon the self.
The wise one should permeate himself with the seed-syllable *haṃsa*;
the knower should flood with nectar that which is situated within the center of the body.
With that nectar, the discerning one should then flood all the limbs.
Having abandoned the ordinary state of being, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.

First, one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), and after that, the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). One should purify the two surfaces of the palms with the *astra-mantra*.
The placement beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger is declared to be the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (the rite of emanation);
that which begins with the little finger and ends with the thumb is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (the rite of withdrawal).

The placement beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (creation placement); that beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna is called the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution placement).

The wise one should place the ten seed-syllables starting from the right thumb and ending with the little finger on the other [hand]; thereafter, he should perform the placement for stability (*sthitinyāsa*). Then, he should place the limbs (*aṅga*) in sequence, beginning with the middle finger and ending with the index finger.
Thus should the ritual placement of Śiva’s limbs (śivāṅganyāsa) be performed on every auspicious festival day.
One should perform the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) by way of [the aforementioned] path;
