for one who is without a wife and remains in a state of celibacy, the ritual placement of withdrawal (*saṃhāranyāsa*) is prescribed.
The creation [mantras] beginning with the head are performed, while the dissolution [mantras] begin with the feet. One should place Īśa upon that head... one should place [the others].
One should then place the two mantras on the feet; thereafter, one should assign the limbs:
the *śikhā* on the crest and the *kavaca* between the breasts.
One should place Locanā in the eyes and Astra in the region of the hands;
the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the thirty-eight Kalās according to the prescribed rite.

One should assign the digits of Īśāna: *Om* to the head, above the forehead; *Ī* to the right ear, above the throat; and *Śā* to the left ear, above the pedestal. (4th line) *Om īśānassarvavidyānāṃ śaśinyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ, the Lord of all beings, salutations to Aṅgadā. (5th line) Oṃ, the sovereign of Brahman, the supreme lord of Brahman, salutations to Brahmādhiṣṭhā.
Oṃ, may there be auspiciousness for me; salutations to Marīci.
Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva-jvālinī.
One should assign the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna to the head and other parts:
[the first] on the faces, [the second] on the right ear, [the third] on the navel, and [the fourth] on the left ear. (Verse 6)
One should place the parts of Tatpuruṣa upon forty locations:
Oṃ, we know Tatpuruṣa; salutation to Peace (Śānti).
Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation to Knowledge (Vidyā).
Oṃ, salutation to Rudra for the sake of installation; Oṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti for the sake of impelling. One should assign the portions of Tatpuruṣa to the four directions, beginning with the face.
O child, one should place the digits of Aghora on the heart, the throat (………), the navel, the back, and indeed the chest. *Oṃ*, salutation to the most terrible Māyā.
Oṃ, obeisance to the non-terrible ones for the sake of delusion; Oṃ, obeisance to the non-terrible protection; (third line) Oṃ, obeisance to those even more non-terrible for the sake of finality.
Oṃ, salutation to all-encompassing death.
Oṃ, salutation to all forms of illusion.
Oṃ, salutation be unto you, O Rudra, salutation to those who are fearsome. (4th line)
Oṃ, salutation to Rūpā and Jarā;
one should install the digits (kalās) of Aghora in the eight corners starting from the heart.
One should place the Vāmadeva-kalās upon the penis and the linga, the thighs, the knees, and also the shanks; likewise upon the buttocks, the hips, and the sides.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to old age.
Oṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭha; salutation to protection. (Sixth line) Oṃ, salutation to Rudra; salutation to pleasure.
Oṃ, homage to Kāla; homage to Pālī. Oṃ, homage to [Kala]…; homage to Vikaraṇa.
Oṃ, salutation to Saṃyaminī. (7th line) Oṃ, salutation to Balakriya. Oṃ, salutation to Vikaraṇa; salutation to Buddhi.
Oṃ, homage to Balakārī! Oṃ, homage to Pramathana, homage to Dhātṛ! Oṃ, homage to Sarvabhūtadamana, homage to Bhrāmiṇī! (F.28a)
Oṃ, salutation to Manomohinī.
Oṃ, salutation to Unmanā; salutation to Bhavā.
On the thirteenth [tithi], one should assign the digits of Vāmadeva to the penis and the other [limbs]. (Second line)
One should assign the *sadyojāta* kalā to both feet, both hands, the arms, the nose, the mouth, and the head. (Third line) *Oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi siddhyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ, salutation indeed to Sadyojāta; salutation to Ṛddhi. Oṃ, salutation to Bhava’s splendor; salutation to Bhava’s fortune. (4th line)
Oṃ, salutation to Medhā in beginningless existence.
Oṃ, accept me; salutation to Kānti.
Oṃ, become [my sustenance]; salutation to Svadhā.
Om, salutation to Udbhava; salutation to Dhṛti. (In the fifth line:
One should place the Sadyojāta-kalā upon the eight locations beginning with the feet.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the sake of others during worship, but for one's own sake, one should place the syllables.
Listen, O Six-faced One, as I shall now explain the arrangement of the syllables:
one should place the *mātṛkā*, beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Kṣa'.
In the two eyes, the two ears, the two cheeks,
the two nostrils, and the two rows of teeth—
one should place sixteen vowels in the apertures of the head.
The *ka*-group [of consonants] is on the right hand, and the *ca*-group on the left;
the *ta*-group is on the right foot and the *ta*-group on the left foot;
*pa* and *pha* are on the right side, while *ba* and *bha* shine upon the left side.
One should place the letter *ma* at the region of the throat...
[the wise practitioner] should place the letter *kṣa* at the region of the genitals.
Having cast off the ordinary state, he should contemplate: "I am Śiva."
Having done this, one should especially perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
One should arrange the ritual procedure in the heart and the fire-oblation (homa) at the navel.
Having meditated on the syllable *Cīḥ* on the forehead, which has the form of smokeless light.
The manifest, the unmanifest, and likewise that which is both manifest and unmanifest.
The wise one should meditate upon Maheśvara as both with parts and without parts, and likewise Śiva and Brahmā; however, he should contemplate the partless Śiva and Brahmā as abiding within Śiva.
I shall now relate it all; listen, O Six-faced One!
[It is] like pure crystal, with a luster as white as cow’s milk.
Three-eyed and ten-armed, peaceful, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
possessing three faces and three heads, and decorated with all ornaments;
the god wearing divine garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
The god is seated in the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana), resting upon a white lotus.
The god who has a bull for his vehicle, who bears a trident and an axe,
and likewise holds a sword and a bell, as well as a thunderbolt and a lance.
The god Maheśa, the lord of the mountains, who bears fire and serpents,
resembles a thousand suns and is like pure crystal.
Endowed with sixteen arms, five faces, and three eyes,
with three eyes upon each face and adorned upon the fifth head;
joined with a sacred thread and decorated with all ornaments.
And he saw the Supreme Lord with his silken garments and fine cloths torn to pieces.
Adorned with golden forehead-plates and all kinds of jewels,
the Supreme Lord was further embellished by five severed heroic arrows.
Adorned with fivefold armlets and embellished with all kinds of jewels,
he was mounted upon a white lotus graced with a thousand petals.
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Gautamī, Narmadā,
Sarasvatī, Sarayū, and Gaṇḍakī, with their hands joined by chowries, [waited upon him].
(7th line) His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and he was adorned with hanging garlands of celestial flowers.
With *kalpavṛkṣa* [trees] and *campaka* flowers...
With *jāti*, *vakula*, and *mandāra* flowers, especially with the five-fold crest;
his limbs are pervaded by the nine powers, O Lord...
Vāmadeva is in the north, along with Vipula and Śikhī;
above that, it is joined with three crests, and above that is Tripura.
O Six-faced One, it is variegated with five jewels upon its five heads.
The southern face is well-favored, while the eastern one faces away;
the western is the other, and the northern shall be the face.
With its face turned upwards, it is situated in the northeastern direction;
one should visualize it as five-faced, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise.
Having placed Īśāna on the head and Puruṣa on the eastern face,
one should place Aghora on the southern face and Sadyojāta on the western side.
One should assign the northern face with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Crystal, saffron, black [pigment], cow’s milk, and the Japā flower—
thus are the colors and mantras of the five faces proclaimed.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the lords of the gods, are the cause of all causes.
Maheśvara is the heart; Sadāśiva is the station in the region of the navel.
In the eternal station of Śiva is the Supreme Brahman, Sadāśiva.
The stalk, however, is the size of a fresh lotus bud;
it is as subtle as half of half of twelve [units], consisting of twenty parts of half a *devī*.
The form that sports with sense objects is like Rūpavatī, possessing all natures;
one should worship her specifically within the twenty-seven obscurations,
and subsequently the five obscurations within the heart-lotus.
And likewise with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense, lamps, and water for the guest-offering (arghya).
With curd, milk, ghee, and the like, as well as with offerings of honey,
the wise man should meditate upon Maheśa with a purely mental disposition.
Thus, Sadāśiva himself, along with the seed and sprout of Śakti and so forth, is declared to be the internal organ; now hear from me the purification of the locations.
Having drawn a mandala one cubit in size before Śiva,
the preceptor should then invoke the Earth, adorned with all ornaments.
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings by means of the heart-mantra,
one should begin the clearing of the directions with the weapon-mantra alone.
The purification of the place has been described; now hear about the purification of the materials.
One should wash the arghya vessel, the shallow bowl, the vessel for water for the feet, the vessel for sipping water, the conch, and the water jars with the weapon mantra (astra-mantra).
The sowing [of the seed-syllables] with the five Brahmans and the seed-syllables of [the Lord] Ṣaṇmukha;
one should purify that [site] with the Astra-mantra and enclose it with the Kavaca-mantra.
[One should perform the rite] joined with the Brahmans, Śiva, Vidyā, and the Aṅgas.
That water has become Śiva himself; it is praised as the mantra of mantras.
One should sprinkle the substances prepared [for the rite] with *kuśa* grass, dropping them drop by drop while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
In this way, the purification of the substances is accomplished; now listen to the procedure for the worship of the gateway.
Nandika and Kāla are established as the guardians of the eastern gate;
likewise, Dindi and Muṇḍa are the guardians of the southern gate;
and Bhṛṅgīśa and Vijaya are the guardians of the western gate.
The guardians of the northern gate are Ananta and Paśupati;
Nandin, who is of dark complexion, is established on the right.
Mahākāla, with the luster of saffron, is established in the north;
Daṇḍī, with the brilliance of Indra’s wrath, is likewise stationed in the south. One should place Muṇḍī, who has a white form, in the left portion.
One should place Bhṛṅgī on the right side in sequence, with a peacock’s neck as his mount;
having placed Vijaya on the left, joined with coral-colored [gems],
one should install Ananta, who has the form of gold, on the right side.
The wise one should place Paśupati, who is blue in color, on the left;
Nandīśa should hold a staff in his hand, and Kāla should carry an axe.
Daṇḍīśa holds a sword in his hand, while Muṇḍīśa carries a skull-bowl;
Bhṛṅgī shall have a spear in his hand, and Vijaya is the bearer of a trident.
Ananta, Vajrahasta...
[all] should be depicted with two arms and holding water-pots;
they should be endowed with all ornaments and adorned with crowns and other finery.
It was joined with waist-bands, anklets, and severed lotus stalks.
Endowed with such characteristics, they are established at each and every door;
at the door of the innermost maṇḍala, Nanda and Kaula are established.
One should worship Bhuvaṅga, Pataṅga, and the deities beginning with Ulikā, as well as Vimala and Subāhu, upon the two door-panels.
One should worship Skandadeva in the middle of that lintel;
one should worship Gaṇapati on the right side above the door. (5th line) One should worship Sarasvatī on the left side above the door.
One should worship Śrīdevī above the door and in its center.
On the right side of the door, the wise one should worship Nandin and Gaṅgā;
on the left side of the door, Mahākāla and Yamunā.
One should first worship the Bull with perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order;
within that area, Bhṛṅgīśa and Vijaya should be worshipped in sequence.
One should construct [the shrines] with boundary walls; likewise, Ananta and Paśupati, along with Kumbhodara and Mahodara, should be joined with great gopuras.
At the end, one should cause the two very powerful [deities] with staffs in hand to be placed in their elemental positions.
Such is the procedure for the worship of the door; now hear the ritual for the worship of the retinue.
[One should worship] the bull, white in color, with black horns, and of great strength.
Possessing a divine form and great beauty, with the complexion of molten gold.
Clad in red garments, terrifying, with hair standing erect and a topknot,
he is equipped with a spear and a javelin, and adorned with a garland of young flowers.
Mounted upon a goat from the fire-ritual, surrounded by the seven tongues of flame,
resembling the whiteness of cow’s milk, with two arms and two eyes.

One should fashion Rohitacandra, who is endowed with a circle of rays, adorned with a crown of lapis lazuli, and holding a white water-lily in his hand. (4th line) I shall now describe the characteristics of the Mothers according to their colors, vehicles, and emblems.
One should fashion Bhadreśa seated in the lotus posture; his characteristics are now described.
Having the luster of the color of a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, dark-complexioned, and holding an axe;
four-armed, with a beautiful face, and seated upon a banyan tree.
Four-faced and large-eyed, with [a complexion like] molten gold...
four-armed, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a water-pot, and a rosary;
bearing a swan-banner, mounted upon a swan, and wearing a crown of matted locks.
The wise man should have an image of Brahmāṇī fashioned from the wood of the Palāśa tree;
she has three eyes, is white in color, holds a trident in her hand, has the bull as her emblem,
grants boons and fearlessness with her hands, and is endowed with a rosary of beads.

The wise man should have the Great Goddess fashioned together with a sandalwood tree—she who is adorned by the Lord of the Earth, whose crown is matted hair, and who is united with Maheśvara. (Verse 8)
Adorned with a cock-banner,
(……………), joined with a lotus, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
mounted upon a strong [vehicle], and resting upon an udumbara tree.
One should have the goddess fashioned wearing linen garments.
(……….. Queen Dhara-devī has hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is endowed with a crown and diadem, and adorned with necklaces and armlets.

One should have the goddess Vaiṣṇavī fashioned—sustaining, with a beautiful face, dark-complexioned, and large-eyed; the queen seated upon a rājavṛkṣa tree and joined by the one whose banner is Garuḍa. Now hear concerning Vārāhī.
She is blue in color, possesses a magnificent form, and is radiant with a crown of jewel-caskets.
Clad in black garments, with tusks and a face like that of a boar,
she holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands, and is accompanied by the Karadruma tree.
Adorned with the lion-banner and decorated with all ornaments,
she was likewise equipped with a parasol and chowries;
radiant with a crown and tiara, her complexion like a circle of jewels.
Joined with Vajrapāśa and united with the wish-fulfilling tree.
The wise one should have the goddess Indrāṇī fashioned, adorned with divine flowers;
he should have Cāmuṇḍī fashioned, possessing a luster like a dark rain-cloud.
Holding a trident and a skull, she is dark-complexioned and four-armed;
her hair stands upright, she is adorned with conch shells, and she is not veiled.
Endowed with the prescribed banner and seated beneath a banyan tree, one should worship Vighneśa, making her possessed of all auspicious characteristics.
The characteristics of the Mothers have been declared; now hear the characteristics of Vighneśa.
He has the face of an elephant, three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms.
In his right hand is a noose and in his left an elephant goad and a sweetmeat;
he has a serpent as a sacred thread, drooping lips, and is the Lord of the Gaṇas.
The characteristics of Vidhneśa have been declared; now hear the characteristics of Kumāra:
resembling the rising sun, eternally possessing the form of a child, four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with all ornaments.
Adorned with necklaces and armlets, and likewise having a peacock as his vehicle.
Resembling coral, with twenty arms, wearing garments the color of mercury,
he holds in his right hands the spear, arrow, sword, the gesture of fearlessness, banner, and mace;
in his left hands there should be the curse-gesture, the axe, and the lower armlet.
On the excellent lotus of Śūla, he has the form of the six-faced one;
he is saffron-colored, endowed with four arms, holding a spear, granting boons, and wearing a bracelet.
The right hand holds Akṣapāda and others, and this Kumāra stands upon a lotus; thus the characteristics of the Youth have been described. Now hear of the goddess Jyeṣṭhā.
Accompanied by a maiden and a son, and marked with the banner of a crow.
One should have the goddess fashioned as wearing red garments, adorned with pearl ornaments,
endowed with all types of jewelry, and accompanied by her husband.
The characteristics of Jyeṣṭhā have been declared; now the characteristics of Durgā are being described:
she is well-attired, has dark hair, and possesses the form of a blue lotus petal.
She has a face like a sacrificial oblation (*caru*), is adorned with all ornaments,
possesses four arms— one of which is in the boon-granting (*varada*) gesture—
and her breasts are bound together; she stands upon the head of Mahiṣa.
The characteristics of Durgā have been declared; now hear those of Bhāskara.
Divine in form, beloved by the world, resembling the calyx of a lotus,
endowed with a halo of light, possessing a neck like a conch shell, and having beautiful eyes.

One should depict him as having the form of the Sun, endowed with all ornaments, possessing great luster, holding lotuses in both hands, adorned with a crown and a casket, and joined with Uṣā and Satyabhāmā.
Holding a beautiful, red lotus in his pair of hands, he wears a garment and a bodice made of perfected coral and gold, possessing auspicious luster;
he is adorned with jeweled earrings, necklaces, armlets, ear-flowers, and a casket.
Bestowing eternal awakening, possessing the splendor of the sun and the creator of the universe,
it should be worshipped by the wise in the northeastern quarter of the sacred field.
It is declared to be threefold according to the division of the three qualities:
the sattvic is white in form, while the rājasic is red in color.
The Tāmasa [form] is black in color and is declared to be of three kinds;
in the Tāmasa [form], it is said to have six arms, while the Rājasa [form] likewise has six arms. (Line 7) As for the Sāttvika [form], it specifically has four arms according to the prescribed rule.
The trident, skull-bowl, axe, and noose are known as his weapons.
His hair stands upright, his face and eyes are beautiful, his eyebrows are full of vigor, and his body has well-curled tips; he is adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Naked in form, with three eyes, and adorned with anklets on his feet;
the glorious one stands upon a dog, endowed with eight arms.
In the right hands [he holds] a trident, a noose, a sword, and a khaṭvāṅga;
in the left hands, a skull-cup, an axe, a shield, and a bell.
He should be surrounded by Vetālas and hosts of Bhūtas, with dogs at his side.
One endowed with these characteristics is known as Kṣetrapāla.
Then, one should especially worship him while he is stationed on a pedestal in front [of the deity].
The Pakṣas, Rākṣasas, Paiśācas, Bhūtas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras; the Pitṛs, Dānavas, and Nāgas— up to Brahmā, Īśāna, and Antaka—
one should [offer] their own names in the middle, preceded by the Praṇava and ending in the dative case.

One should append "to all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*) to the instruction for the offering (*balinirdeśa*) ending in *svāhā*. (6th line) A brick pedestal (*iṣṭikā-pīṭha*) and an earthen pedestal (*mṛtpīṭha*) are said to be the appearance of the pedestal (*pīṭhābhāsa*).
The mind that perceives appearances becomes like wood or clay;
among these, that which is made of clay is superior to that which is made of wood, and likewise, that which is made of metal is superior to that which is made of clay.
Among those made of metal, stone is superior; likewise, among those made of stone, gemstone is superior. One should have the primary image (mūlabera) fashioned from stone, gems, and metals.
It should be made with the finest materials available; one should not do otherwise.
The worship of the retinue has been declared; now hear concerning the purification of the liṅga.
Having then entered the inner sanctum, one should perform the purification of the liṅga.
One should then offer water for the feet and other offerings, and worship it properly with the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should offer the flower worshipped during the morning twilight to Īśāna;
with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger, the fresh flower is released.
With the thumb and forefinger, one should sprinkle and then dismiss [the deity];
at the time of dismissal, one should place that flower upon the head.
One should indeed wash the *liṅga* with the *liṅga-mantra* using the palm of the right hand;

one should wash the pedestal (*pīṭha*) all around in sequence with the *pāśupatāstra-mantra*. In this way, the purification of the *liṅga* is accomplished; thereafter follows the purification of the mantra.

All mantras, especially those beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, should be employed in the sacrifice; such is the declared purity of the mantra. He who knows the fivefold purity is worthy to perform the worship.

If one performs a sacrifice during the transit [of a planet], one shall obtain that result as fruitless. (7th line) When the Moon and Sun have vanished, a sacrifice is auspicious and brings about all accomplishments.

When one sneezes, [the breath] has transferred; thus, from the emission (*visarga*) until the end of the equinox (*viṣuvant*), if one sneezes at the time of the emission, the sacrifice shall be fruitless.
When the sun is at the equinox or during a transit, worship should never be performed [in the usual manner].
One should worship the Lord while standing either facing the southeast (Agni) or the southwest (Nirṛti).
There, one should prepare a seat according to the procedure seen in the scriptures, not by mere ritual action.
The support is declared to be the seat (āsana), and that which is supported is Supreme Śiva.
The *nāda* is called the *liṅga*, and the *bindu* is remembered as the *pīṭha*.
There is no *Śakti* without *Śiva*, nor is there a *Śiva* devoid of *Śakti*.

It is to be known as being like fragrance in flowers, and likewise like oil in sesame seeds; it is like sound in musical instruments, and all heat is likewise that of fire. (4th line) It is like fire in wood, and likewise like sap in fruits.
Just as the power of the vital breath resides within bodies, one should therefore worship the liṅga.
Power alone is declared to be the seat; these five seats are taught in sequence:
the terrestrial egg, then the stalk, and finally that which ends with fire.
Then the Nandyāsana is proclaimed, and the Siṃhāsana is the second;
the Yogāsana is the third, and the Padmāsana is the fourth.
The fifth is indeed named Vimala; these [five] consist of the nature of the five elements.
It is circular in shape, infinite, and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
One should visualize it below and fashion a lion-throne above.
Knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty—this is the fourfold [set].
The color of the [deities] beginning with Dharmā should be white, ruby-red, golden, and the luster of emerald, respectively, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and proceeding in order.
One should visualize the four feet in the form of lions at the four corners—
[the goddess] whose face is formidable with fangs, who has three eyes, and who takes the form of the earth.
Each [of these] is surrounded by lions numbering in the millions and so forth;
likewise, Adharma, Ignorance, Non-detachment, and Non-mastery—
[all] resembling lapis lazuli— one should arrange them in the directions starting from the east.
By means of the three-fold guru, today indeed this shall become the lion-throne (siṃhāsana).
(Line 5) This is known as the lion-throne; beyond this is the yoga-posture.
[Therein] are the vital airs: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya; these are known as the Yogāsanas. Now listen to the Padmāsana.

Born and situated within the lotus-womb, with seven steps in the center, one should cause the deceased to enter that place; one should cause him to enter the Śakti. (7th line) The Māyā-tattva is vast and fragrant, adorned by the lotus of Śuddhavidyā. (F.35b)
It is white, endowed with eight petals, and joined with filaments in the form of śaktis.
There, one should worship the pericarp consisting of the reality of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*);
its seed-syllable has the luster of coral, and its sprout has the brilliance of silver. Its stalk is of lapis lazuli, and the pericarp is reddish-brown.
The tip of the petal, which is conch-white in color, is known as the red lower petal.
The filaments in the center should be somewhat red and yellow;
in their midst, the wise one should fashion the pericarp, which has the luster of gold.
With *sadyojāta* one should [visualize] the root of the lotus, with *vāmadeva* the stalk,
(line 4) with *aghora* the petals interspersed, and with *tatpuruṣa* the secret filaments.
The lotus, ending at the pericarp, is Īśāna;
likewise, the lotus situated within the womb of power (*śaktiyoni*) has a mobile liṅga in its center. The stalk of the lotus is the Śiva-liṅga, the Great Lord who pervades all.
I shall now describe this Yonipīṭha, which accomplishes all desires and goals. (Line 6) One should place Vāmaśakti in the southeast, Jyeṣṭhāśakti in the southwest,
Raudrī in the northwest, and likewise Ambikā in the northeast.
Sukhāmadhī is in the eastern direction; likewise, Śubhākṣī is in the south (7th line);
Bhāgāyī is in the southern (western) quarter; and Bhagadarpaṇī is in the north.
One should worship the Bhagas and those of dark complexion with their respective initial names;
the power of the cardinal directions is white in color, while the power of the intermediate directions is red in color.

One should face the principal [deity] while endowed with this form: three-eyed, four-armed, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. One should know that the pedestal is made square and possesses its characteristic shape and color.
Above that, one should place a sixteen-petalled lotus of even circumference.
One should worship its sixteen petals;
in the middle of each petal, one should worship the seed-syllable resembling the color of milk, adorned with the sound of the ocean.
One should know the lotus as the radiance; above that is the triple mandala:
namely, fire, the sun, and the lunar mandala.
The base is the fire-triangle, and the remainder is indeed three concentric circles;
these should be fashioned in their proper order and worshipped with their respective seed-syllables.
In the center of the triangular mandala, the triple-linga is well-established by the gods.
Then, one should worship the red [syllable] in the middle of the three genders.
One should worship that which is upon the yoni within the spaces of the hairs. Above that, however, is the Vāgbhava [syllable], which has the brilliance of the rising sun.
Endowed with the Bindu and Nāda, it is Śakti, the subtle and supreme Śiva;
this seed-syllable consists of Śiva and Śakti, and likewise of Umā and Rudra.
[She who is] the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all beings, both moving and unmoving;
three-eyed and four-armed, consecrated for the sport of bliss;
resembling pure crystal, with beautiful breasts and in the full bloom of youth.
Adorned with pearl ornaments, dressed in white garments, and most beautiful;
seated in the vīrāsana posture, wearing a crown and earrings;
the yoni-mudrā on the right, and above it a garland.
The wise know that the goddess on the left, with a hand full of nectar, should hold a book;
this is the form of the Goddess as Śiva in his gross, subtle, and supreme aspects.
One should worship with nine flowers according to the path of the five obstructions;
one should also worship the lineage gurus and perform the veneration of their sandals.
Facing north, the wise one should meditate upon all [the forms]:
the Liṅga situated in the embrace of Umā, the head, and the navel arise. (5th line) Mahādeva exists as the Liṅga within the seven cosmic eggs of everyone.
The wise man should worship the infinite one known as the Śivaliṅga.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
each of these should be worshipped by the preceptor according to their respective portions with their corresponding mantras.
One should worship the Liṅga situated within; having performed the supreme rites of invocation and dismissal,

and having placed the joined palms at the heart with a flower while reciting the Prāsāda-mantra according to one's capacity, the practitioner attains a state of equanimity, becoming one with the partless (niṣkala) sphere of experience.
One should meditate sequentially upon the ray of one's own power (*svaśakti*), then upon the resonance (*nāda*), and likewise upon the point (*bindu*).
Once proficiency has been attained in this sequence within the abode of one's own power, there should be the invocation of the God.
When the embryo situated within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) and Śiva situated within the *liṅga* [are perceived], [the invocation is complete].
The individual soul, resting in the maternal side, is full of the nature of the Self;
it is fit for devotion, mantra, and ritual action, while Śiva is the partless presence.
(3rd line) Having formed a handful of flowers and being permeated by the true being of Śiva, [one should offer them].
One should proceed in sequence from the three measures (*trimātra*) up to the primordial sound (*nāda*) and so forth.
Just as fire, though present within wood, remains hidden until it blazes forth through friction, O Guha,
so too does [the inner fire] manifest through devotion, dispassion, and being bound by the rope of mantra.
Just as the manifestation of that fire [is not obstructed] by the root-knot within the wood,
so too the manifestation of the one, all-pervading consciousness is not impeded.
Just as fire contained within a vessel blazes up when fanned by the wind,
so too is the Lord Śiva manifested through the *liṅga-mantra*.
The subtle body (*liṅga*) of living beings goes to dissolution; it remains established within this [body].

Just as fire situated within wood is perceived even when the wood is reduced to ashes, so too, though the [subtle body] may be diminished, it is found by means of its application within a single part of the wood-like [gross body]. (Verse 7, line 1) Indeed, when situated in one region of the wood, it is smeared over through its pervasive activity.
The mantra-practitioner is all-pervasive like wood; the hundred thousandfold caravan [of phenomena] is like fire.
One should meditate on the object of knowledge as being like wealth; the omnipresent Lord exists like fire.
That which is the deity, both supreme and non-supreme, is called the invocation.
Turning away from it is then called its dismissal (*udvāsana*);
for the consecrated (*śiṣṭa*) liṅga, especially, there is no invocation or dismissal.
Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Maheśa are the threefold forms;
he is devoid of both the expressed and the expression, transcending speech and mind, and beyond the reach of the senses.
Endowed with all the qualities of omniscience, the Lord who is the abode of all principles—

Śiva has declared that one who is thus constituted is proclaimed as "niṣkala" (the partless). (Line 4) The "sakala" (with parts) is endowed with the "niṣkala," consisting of thirty-eight constituent parts (*kalās*).
The path of the kalās is complete with its limbs; the path of the worlds is borne by the hairs of the body as previously described.

The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), together with the skin, is endowed with the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) and blood; the path of words (padādhvan), along with the veins and flesh, consists essentially of honey and pure [nectar].
Sadāśiva is the essence of the six paths; his vital breath is known as Śiva.
(6th line) Complete with the limbs beginning with the heart, he assumes a manifest form in meditation.
In the absence of that [manifestation], it is partless; therefore, the Sakala and Niṣkala forms are one.
I shall now describe specifically the true nature of Sadāśiva:
shining like jasmine, the moon, and crystal, adorned with matted locks and a crown.
Among them, he has five faces, each with three eyes;
he is adorned with all ornaments and endowed with ten arms.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a vajra, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Holding a noose, a serpent, a bell, and fire, and granting boons with his left [hands],
the god wears celestial garments and is adorned with divine flowers.
At the time of worship, the wise one should meditate upon the Linga in its center as having limbs anointed with divine perfumes, a peaceful form, and a smiling countenance;
on the pedestal (piṇḍikā), he should meditate upon the Goddess, who possesses a divine form and is beyond the reach of the mind (manonmanī).
The goddess Manonmanī, radiant as a pearl, holds a noose and a goad;
she is in the full bloom of youth, well-attired, with beautiful breasts and a slender waist,
possessing a neck like a conch shell and well-proportioned limbs, and is surrounded by the nine Śaktis.
The goddess Vāmā is like the color of a forest fire, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
Jyeṣṭhā is yellow in complexion, holding a lotus, and has lotus-like eyes.
The goddess Raudrī resembles Raudra; she has three eyes and holds a trident.
The goddess [Kālī] resembles gold; she holds a mallet.

Kalavikaraṇī is smoke-colored, holding a noose in her hand, and in the full bloom of youth; Śvetā, the Balavikaraṇī, is white, wielding a sword, and possesses great strength. (Line 7) The goddess Balapramathanī holds a palāśa staff.
And [there is] Sarvabhūtadamani, who is red in color and carries a skull-cup.
One should place the coverings of the pedestal, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna;
one should worship them with perfumes and flowers using their respective name-mantras.
One should establish the Ātma-tattva everywhere; however, O gentle one, one should especially worship the Śiva-tattva in the center, while the Vidyā-tattva is [to be worshipped] in the north. 160.
The wise one should place the Śiva-tattva, which has Rudra as its presiding deity, in the middle,
whether it resides in the liṅgas or in the kautuka.
Even when the linga and so forth are not present, whether on a mandala or upon a sacrificial mound (sthandila),
the invocation through prayer is traditionally prescribed by means of the Samāgatā mantra.
"Seated upon this seat"—thus is the ritual of installation (sthāpana);
they know that the welcoming with the appropriate mantra is the ritual of facing [the deity] (samukhīkaraṇa).
"Forgive this sequence," thus [one says], and having obtained permission for the invocation;
at the base of the *liṅga* is the reality (*tattva*), while the face is said to be at the tip of the thread.
The knower of mantras should place the two threads on the sides of the cloth with his arms, and the back-part upon the knot of the thread;
then, by means of the Sadyojāta mantra, he should invoke the deity.
One should perform the installation with the *Dvāmadeva* mantra, the presence (*sannidhi*) with the *Aghora*,
the removal of disease with the *Puruṣa*, and victory with the *Īśāna*.
Likewise, the face in the west or the north [is worshipped];
with the Aghora mantra, one faces south, and the Tatpuruṣa face is in the east.
The upper face is Īśāna; thus it is remembered as the five-faced one.
To the left [of the central face] are the conch, cow’s milk, and a blue lotus and a white lotus.
One should contemplate the Person who is non-terrible, dark as collyrium, radiant as saffron,
and possessing a face with five colors, shining like crystal, the lord Ishana.
One should know that Vāmadeva is Brahmā, Janārdana is Sadyojāta,
and Manonmanī is the supreme essence of Sadāśiva.
One should offer water for washing the feet (pādya) once each time, beginning with the right foot and ending with the left;
one should then offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the [guest's] mouths with an uninterrupted stream of water.
One should offer the arghya water once upon the head, apply fragrant paste to the limbs,
and perform an ablution on the head with pure water and other such substances.
Standing either before the fire or before Nirṛti, one should worship the God;
the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed, and one should cause it to be offered upon the head of Śiva.
For Śiva who has arrived here, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) at his feet with the heart-mantra;
one should give water for sipping (ācamana) into his mouth, and one should cause the water of honor (arghya) to be given to Śiva’s face.
One should perform the deposition of the thirty-eight *kalās* in the sequence beginning with the crown (*makuṭa*);
one should recite the five Brahmans along with the limbs of Śiva and the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra.
Thereafter, one should establish [the deity] with water, and likewise with curd,
milk, ghee, coconut water, honey, and the five products of the cow (brahmapañcaka).
One should bathe the supreme liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the Brahmakūrca mixture,
using the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya), as well as with ground śāli rice.
Having bathed it with auspicious water, one should rub it with fragrant paste;
thereafter, one should rub it with turmeric and bathe it with scented water.
After that, the wise one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the five faces;
then, having especially prepared the pedestal of the liṅga, he should smear it with cloth.
One should cause the flower to be placed upon the head with the heart-mantra;
one should strike the bell there and likewise cast aside the curtain.
One should cause the garment, the sacred thread, the perfume, the crown, the earrings,
as well as the necklace, the armlets, and the garland to be offered with the heart-mantra.
Having offered incense and lamps from the heart,
thereafter one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) at the time of dusk for the sake of averting the world's impurity that defiles the eyes.
One should perform the protection of the western direction and the offering of incense before the cloth;
then, one should prepare a square mandala in front of the linga or in front of the image.
Having fashioned five faces and grasped the [five] hearts, one should place them;
one should sprinkle [them] with the *puruṣa* [mantra] and display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
One should indeed fashion a lamp-stand out of rice flour,
with a width of four finger-breadths and a height of two finger-breadths.
The best [wick] is said to be half a finger in length and shaped like the full moon;
one should place a lamp in its center and lamps in the four directions and the middle.
One should arrange these five lamps together with cow’s ghee.
Having worshipped the lamp-stand, the best of preceptors should cause it to be prepared.
One should worship with mustard seeds, salt, cotton, and so forth,
as well as with perfumes, flowers, and incense, using the heart-mantra alone.
Having worshipped the fire according to the rules with the seed-syllable of fire,
the wise one [should proceed] amidst the sounding of conchs and drums and the utterances of auspicious words.
The wise one should first offer water for the feet with the Astra-mantra, then give water for sipping (ācamana) with the Netra-mantra;
having whirled it three times with the Dīpa-mantra, he should then use the Śikhā-mantra.
Repeating this again and again according to the sequence of substances,
one should perform three revolutions with the *liṅga* on the head and likewise three revolutions with the feet.
The wise practitioner should rotate the three-fold *ārati* from the knees up to the crown of the head;
he should cause the ashes to be applied [to the body] and perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) for Śambhu with the *astra-mantra*.
One should cause the protective cord to be tied with the tip of the ring finger;
it may be performed by Rudra, or by courtesans, or by the [deities] beginning with Pātra and Asura.
Then, one should place a fire-lamp together with all kinds of musical instruments at the front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), and one should especially cause it to be prepared.
The wise man should not burn here with the fire of a lamp, even if it be royal, seasonal, made of cotton, white, or mustard-seed, using the seed-syllable of fire.
One should fan the face with yak-tail whisks and other fans,
cover it from above with an umbrella, and show a mirror to the face.
The ten mudrās should be applied as described upon the ten hands;
the vajra and so forth, ending with the lotus mudrā, are proclaimed as the ten mudrās.
Now hear about the fifth enclosure, which is called the Nirājana.
The science of embryology, Gaṇeśa, and the weapons of the world-protectors.
The fivefold enclosure has been described for the sake of bestowing all prosperity;
the wise man [should perform it] specifically at the root of the lotus within the enclosure of the womb.

One should worship the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) in the center of the lotus, the Gaṇeśas at half that [distance], the world-protectors (Lokapālas) on the tips of the petals, and the weapons (astras) outside them.
One should worship Tatpuruṣa in the east and Aghora in the south;
one should worship Sadyojāta in the west and Vāmadeva in the north.
One should worship Īśāna above the liṅga with perfumes and flowers;
having worshipped the Heart-mantra in the southeast (pāvaka), one should sacrifice to the Śikhā-mantra in the southwest (nirṛti).
One should worship the armor (kavaca) in the region of the wind (the northwest), the head in the domain of Īśa (the northeast),
the weapon (astra) in the south, and one should worship the eye in the northeast.
One should perform the worship of the womb-enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) at the base of the petals;
[one should worship] Śukra, Ratna, Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the one with a yellow luster resembling milk.
The five Brahmās should be fair-complexioned, three-eyed, and four-armed;
they are equipped with an axe and a trident, and are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
It is said that the form of Īśāna is peaceful, while that of Aghora is remembered as fierce;
their respective colors are white, yellow, reddish, black, and dark red.
They are colored [according to their respective directions], possess six limbs, three eyes, and four arms.
This is indeed the first enclosure; now hear of the second enclosure.
Ananteśa, as well as Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and Ekanetra, [are located there].
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin.
These eight Lords of the Vidyās are three-eyed and four-armed;
they are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and are equipped with an axe and a trident.
Red, white, blue, yellow, black, saffron,
and the color of vermilion resembling collyrium— these are the colors of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) in sequence.
One should worship specifically from Indra up to Īśāna;
thus is the enclosure of the Vidyeśvaras. Now hear about the enclosure of the Gaṇeśvaras.
One should worship Gaurī in the north, and one should worship the Bull in the east;
one should worship Gaṇeśa in the direction of Yama (the southwest), and indeed one should worship Guha in the western direction.
Having worshipped Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, and the supreme Caṇḍa in the corners beginning with the southeast according to the prescribed rule, one should proceed.
Two-eyed and two-armed, Śyāmā is fair-complexioned; she holds a blue lotus in her right hand.
Caṇḍa is also two-eyed and two-armed, dark-complexioned, and holds a chisel in his hand.
[He rides] a white bull of great strength with sharp horns.
One should visualize Nandīśa as four-armed and three-eyed, of dark complexion,
endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and holding an axe and a trident.
Then one should visualize Gajānana (the Elephant-faced) as three-eyed, resembling saffron in hue, and four-armed.
In his right hands, he holds a noose and a tooth, while in his left hands, he holds a goad and a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*).
He has a serpent as his sacred thread, drooping lips, and is the Lord of the Gaṇas. Mahākāla is three-eyed, black in color, and four-armed.
The fearless one, endowed with the power of granting boons, possessing fierce energy, and bearing a trident.
O Mahāsena, he is red in color, with two eyes and four arms;
in his right hands he holds the gesture of fearlessness and the vajra, while in his left hands he holds the gesture of granting boons and the goad.
Bhr̥ṅgīśa has four arms and three eyes, with a tawny complexion;
in his right hands he holds an axe and a trident, while in his left hands he displays the gesture of granting boons and holds a trident.
This is the enclosure of Gaṇeśa; now hear of the enclosure of the World-Guardians (Lokeśas), who possess divine forms, mighty arms, and two eyes upon their faces.
Dark-complexioned, mounted upon an elephant, and surrounded by hosts of apsarases,
he was adorned with divine ornaments and embellished with celestial garlands.
One should depict Vajrapāṇi mounted on a chariot, as Indra, the lord of the gods,
possessing a divine form and great beauty, resembling molten gold.
The god wears red garments, has upward-pointing hair and a topknot,
is joined with a spear, and is adorned with garlands of flames.
One should visualize the Fire-god mounted upon a goat, surrounded by his seven tongues,
and as mounted upon a great buffalo, possessing a luster like that of black collyrium.
One should depict the god holding a staff and a noose, with eyes like blazing fire,
possessing the form of Vaivasvata, wrathful, and terrifying to the world.
[One should visualize] the Lord of Rākṣasas, large-eyed, holding a sword and a shield,
mounted upon a corpse, with a terrifying face, red hair, and in the full bloom of youth.
One should fashion the form of Nirṛti with beautiful tusks and a dark-blue complexion;
he is as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, holds a noose in his hand, possesses great strength,
is adorned with necklaces and armlets, and is embellished by two earrings.
One should fashion a great form situated in a crocodile, having the appearance of Varuṇa.
[Vāyu]— who is ever-moving, smoke-colored, with tawny eyes and fluttering garments,
possessing curved eyebrows, heroic, mounted upon a deer, and endowed with great strength.
One should especially represent Vāyu as adorned with all ornaments,
and Kubera, the king of the Yakṣas, as beautiful in every limb.
One should depict the Lord, the Master of Yakṣas, wearing a variegated crown and adorned with two earrings;
he is graced with necklaces and armlets, mounted upon a horse, and holds a mace;
the god wears crimson garments.
Īśāna, mounted upon a bull and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
One should fashion the form of Īśāna as the white-colored Lord of the Gods, Hara, the three-eyed Lord of the World who holds a trident in his hand.
He has four faces and four arms, carries a water-pot and a sacred thread,
is golden-hued, wears matted hair and a crown, and has a sacrificial thread as his upper garment.
The god is red in color, wearing silken garments, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
the god holds a rosary and a water-pot in his left hand.
Whether he is seated or standing, one should visualize him situated in the lotus posture (padmāsana),
with Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī stationed on both his sides.
Viṣṇu, adorned with a crown and armlets, graced by a sacred sacrificial thread,
resembling a tulasī flower, possessing a prominent nose and auspicious eyes.
One should especially depict Viṣṇu as having two eyes, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, granting fearlessness,
and wearing yellow garments; likewise, Śrī and Bhūmi should be depicted,
along with [the goddess] of dark luster whose body is adorned with a sacred thread.
And one should worship Gaṇeśa between those two for seven measures.
The weapons of the world-protectors are known to range from the vajra to the lotus:
the vajra, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the goad.
The mace, trident, discus, and lotus constitute the ten weapons;
[the colors are] yellow, blue-lotus blue, dark like a rain-cloud, and white.
Padmarāga, tuṣāra, śabala, and śvetarakta;
where there is a spear, a mace, or a noose, [the word] is neuter.
The remaining [deities] have the form of humans, with one face and two hands;
having thus described the weapons and armor, one should worship them beneath the tips of the petals.
Having performed worship specifically with the mantra of each respective name, the fivefold enclosure has thus been described; now hear the ritual services (upacāras).
There are ten services (upacāra) ending with the lamp; sixteen when ending with the oblation (havis);
twenty-five when ending with the offering (bali); and thirty-six up to the end of the tāṇḍava dance.
The invocation, the offering of water for the guest (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), likewise water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
the bath, clothing, the sacred thread, incense, the lamp, and the dismissal.
The worship of Śiva with lamps should be understood as consisting of ten services (daśopacāra):
invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya).
Bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers; incense, lamps, food offerings and the like; prostration and the ritual dismissal.
One should worship with the sixteen types of offerings at the conclusion of the oblation;
having performed the invocation, the ritual bathing, the welcome, and the expression of approval.
Rinsing the mouth, the offering of water (arghya), bathing, garments, the sacred thread,
an upper cloth, ornaments, scents, flowers, as well as incense and lamps.
Then follows the lustration rite (nīrājana), the display of mudrās, the worship of the veils,
the offering of food (naivedya), the performance of the fire sacrifice (homa), and likewise the presentation of the bali offering.
The recitation of hymns, prostrations, the dismissal at the end of the festival, and the rite for peace at the conclusion of the offering—
these are the twenty-five services for the deity.
The seat, the invitation, the water for the guest-offering, the welcome, the respectful salutation,
the water for the feet, the water for sipping, the bath, the garment, and the sacred thread.
Ornaments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, as well as the water-offering (arghya),
the waving of lights (nirājana), collyrium, the fly-whisk, the parasol, and the mirror.

The visualization of the ten mudrās, the worship of the five enclosures, the offering of food, the performance of the fire sacrifice, the presentation of the bali offering, and likewise the recitation of mantras.

Meditative concentration, hymns of praise, recitation, and meditation; likewise, chanting, instrumental music, dance, the offering of water, and the dismissal—these are the thirty-six modes of service.
Thus, at the conclusion of the dance, there is the worship of the deity for the sake of others during the Pauṣika rite;
likewise, at the end of the festival, there is worship with twenty-five services performed at the three junctions of the day.
During half a watch (yāma), the wise one should recite [the mantra] and worship with the eight limbs;
however, he should perform the worship especially without the fire-oblation (homa), the bali-offering, and the festival.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings—
this eightfold worship of the gods stationed in the celestial chariot at the gate-tower continues perpetually until the edge of the rampart.
One should perform the perpetual festival together with the deity residing at that fundamental site.
Worship of Śiva at dawn is beneficial for the twice-born, dear to Brahmā, and conducive to nourishment;
worship of Śiva at midday is beneficial for kings, dear to Viṣṇu, and brings peace;
worship of Śiva in the evening is beneficial for Vaiśyas, dear to Śambhu, and bestows happiness.
For Śūdras, the beneficial [practice] is that of midnight; for Umā’s beloved [the devotee], it may be performed according to desire.
Seven offerings of water, three types of perfumes, an arghya offering, eight incense sticks, lamps, flowers, a canopy, and subsequently the ringing of bells and the scattering of parched grain.

One should properly employ water seven times: for the invocation, the offering of arghya, the foot-washing, the bathing, the sipping of water (ācamana), the presentation of the food offering, and the dismissal.

One should properly apply fragrance during the three occasions of the water-offering (arghya), the unguent, and the bath; likewise, the water-offering is used at the invocation, at the conclusion of the worship, and at the dismissal. [Furthermore, it is used] at the times of offering the seat and worship, at the end of the worship, and at the dismissal.

One should employ the *pracchannapaṭa* (the secret cloth) after it has been cut, at the four times. [Excluded are] one afflicted by a sinful disease, one who has fallen from grace, an atheist, one who reviles the sacred scriptures,
one with missing limbs, one of evil conduct, and likewise one devoid of initiation.
One who neglects the daily rites, one who lacks the sight of a cat,
a Kuṇḍa, a Kolaka, a heretic, and a Śipiviṣṭaka;
Those who sell the Vedas, those who sell sacred texts,
those afflicted with skin diseases such as leprosy, and those who misappropriate the property of Śiva;
One who steals the Guru’s property, one who betrays the Guru, a sinner, one of foul speech, one of evil conduct, a fool, and one who reviles the Guru—
if they should see [the deity] through negligence, their worship shall be fruitless.
Having brought the cloth-painting at the three times of day, [during] bathing, incense, and … ||
During all remaining times, one should wrap [the image] with a cloth;
or else, in another manner, specifically during the time for the cloth.
At the time of worship, one should offer food oblations and then adorn [the deity] with flowers;
at the time of displaying the mudrās, one should employ gold, jewels, and so forth. During such times, one should begin the rite of the concealed cloth (*pracchannapaṭa*).
At the time of beginning the worship, at the end of the worship, and when the offering is presented.
In temples where there are constant festivals and the like, one should strike the great bell.
By the sound of the bell, the Rākṣasas, Asuras, Piśācas, and Brahmarākṣasas depart, and the deity remains in close proximity.
First the water for the feet, and at the end of that, likewise the garment and the sacred thread.
One should offer water for drinking at the beginning of the presentation and dismiss [the deity] at the end;
one should then give the five-fold sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule as is appropriate.
The Vāruṇa, the Saumya, the Āgneya, the Vāyavya, and again the Pārthiva;
then the Vānaspatya is the sixth, while the Prājāpatya is the seventh.
The eighth flower for Śiva should be employed in the worship of Śiva;
it is known as the water-born (lotus) belonging to Varuṇa, while that belonging to Soma is honey, ghee, and milk.
Incense and lamps belong to Agni; fans and such items belong to Vāyu;
bulbs, roots, and the like belong to Pṛthivī (Earth); and fruits and the like belong to Vanaspati (the Lord of Forests).
That which begins with the syllable preceding the end of *prājāpatya* is the *bhāvana* of the beloved’s flower;
one should especially worship each substance while striking the bell.
O Ācārya, through the yoga of ritual action, [the deity] is not present;
however, because of the power of that ritual action, it may be extended—therefore, perform the dismissal of the liberated one.
If one ever performs the rites of incense, lamps, food offerings,
or the worship of the *liṅga* out of delusion, the *brahmarākṣasas* slay him.
One should establish [the deity] with its own tantra and worship it with that same tantra;
if one worships it with another tantra, it will swiftly destroy that village.
Even those who bring benefit to the world will perish, without a doubt;
therefore, one should not cause [such acts] to be performed with all effort.
Constant worship without mantras leads to the state of a *piśāca* (……).
Diseases, thieves, robbers, and the like shall always increase one's fear.
A terrible war would break out for the king, and his mind would always remain distressed;
therefore, with every effort, he should worship [the deity] together with the sacred mantras.
Mantra is to be known as threefold: Vaidika and likewise Tāntrika;
the Tāntrika is threefold, consisting of the methods for Mantra, A-mantra, and Vidhāna.
It is indeed Vedic, Tantric, and likewise Vaidika-Tantric;
performed with Vedic mantras by those following the Veda, and likewise with Tantric mantras by those following the Tantra.
Through Vedic and Tantric mantras, it becomes Vaidika-Tantrika;
or it may be purely Tantrika, Vāma, or Yāmala—thus it is threefold.
The Vaidika [tradition] is also mixed within the Dakṣiṇa-yāmala,
while the Vāma-yāmala-tantra consists of substances, mantras, and various ritual distinctions.
One should perform the rites of the Dakṣiṇāgama with the right hand,
and one should carry out the rites taught in the Vāmatantra with the left hand.
Listen now to the procedure for food offerings known as the "Distinction of Worship" (pūjābheda);
seek that which is beneficial for yourself, having first properly cooked whatever substance is required.
One should cause that wealth, which grants all perfections, to be offered to the Supreme Lord;
for if one consumes it instead of giving it away, that wealth and property will perish.

The food offering (naivedya) is traditionally said to be of three kinds: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). The obligatory [offering] is declared to be of nine types, and likewise the occasional [offering] is of nine.
It has been stated that one may perform the ritual action as desired; here, the distinctions among them are now explained.
An offering made with merely an *āḍhaka* measure is called the lowest of the low.
The smallest and the middlemost [measures] should be one droṇa each;
the lowest of the superior is half a khārī and a bhāra, while half of that is known as the middling.
It is said that the middling-best [oblation] consists of four droṇas of rice;
and the best-lowest oblation is said to be prepared with five droṇas.
That prepared with six *droṇas* of rice is considered middling;
that prepared with eight *droṇas* of rice is said to be the highest of the high.
Thus, the ninefold [classification] of obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites has been declared;
beginning with eight droṇas, it is explained by that same progressive increase.
Thus, the three groups beginning with the lowest consist of twelve bhāras each;
for the occasional [offering], the sacrificial food (naivedya) is declared to be of nine kinds.
That which is measured by those [standard] numbers is called pārthiva; that which is measured by those [same] numbers is called kāmyaka.
Then, a kuḍupa combined with a prastha is said to be paiśāca.
Two *prasthas* are declared to be a *caru*, while one *āḍhaka* is called an oblation (*havis*).
One should not prepare the food offering (*naivedya*) with less than half an *āḍhaka* of rice.
One should know that eight *kuñjas* make a *māṣaka*, and twenty *māṣakas* make a *dharaṇa*. Eight *dharaṇas* make a *pala*, and this is indeed called a *phala*.
Four *hasta*s make one *pāda*; four *pāda*s make one *prastha*;
[four *prastha*s] make one *āḍhaka*; and four of those make one *droṇa*.

The path is indicated as ninefold; one should prepare [the offerings] ending with the *naivedya*. These are, in sequence: *tala*, *prakuñca*, *prasṛti*, *kuḍupa*, *añjali*, *prastha*, *pātra*, *āḍhaka*, *droṇa*, and *khārī*.
But for the śukti, one should count the mantra separately twice over.
Three khāris constitute a bhāra, as does the same measure for grain;
likewise, there are the Hemaśāli, Mahāśāli, and Raktashāli varieties.
White rice, black rice, and the most excellent *saṅganthika*,
as well as bamboo-seed rice and barley, and a small amount of *śālicamādhūri*.
Kustumbarī, nīvāra, and madhyamā are proclaimed [as the first three];
bilāla, sādhāra, vrīhi, and slightly black rice as the sixth.
Likewise, the sūravaīrī and the hrasvavartī are inferior;
for their grain is not fit for the consumption of the Lord.
Having sprinkled [the site] with women born of the four castes who are equal [in merit], along with mortars;
a woman born of the four castes who possesses a husband and sons is considered [fit for this task].
One among them gave birth to a girl named Maṅgalā;
she was devoted to the preparation of rice and endowed with piety.
Having placed grain scorched by the rays of the sun into a mortar,
facing either east or north, one should remove the husks with a pestle; then,
using a winnowing basket, one should discard the broken grains and the chaff.
Two hundred and twenty-five measures of rice suffice for purification.
Having first bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure with excellent attendants,
they should wear white garments and white sacred threads.
All those with purifying grass (pavitra) in their hands should prepare the cooked offerings for the ritual;
one should fill a large water-vessel (jaladroṇa) with water filtered through a cloth.
Then, having purified the vessel, one should wash the rice with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
having performed this six times, one should wash it again and again.
The measure of rice should be equal to half [the amount] of water;
one should cleanse the water and rice with the "mouths of the seed-syllables" (*bījamukha*) using a vessel.
(5th line) The Preceptor should worship the trident with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, using the rice grains.
Having placed the vessel upon his head, he should cast the fire away with the Astra-mantra.
One should kindle the fire with wood that is marked by sparks, covered in ants, infested with worms, or dyed red, and which has been used for a river-crossing.
One should not offer as an oblation food that is infested with hair or insects, mixed with gravel or chaff,
overcooked, or undercooked.
One should offer [the oblation] ending with oil from those [substances] of various colors and scents;
such is the sequence for Śuddhodana. Now hear about milk-rice (pāyasa): one should take twice as much milk as rice, and half as much water.
Mudga beans soaked in half their weight of water are indeed proclaimed to be equal to milk-rice (pāyasa).
Half a measure of rice is prescribed, along with pure mung-bean essence;
at the end of cooking, it should be seasoned with salt, black pepper, and cumin.

When that kṛsarā rice is mixed with sesame powder, it is so designated; it is prepared with one-third part rice and the essence of mung beans. Cooked mung bean porridge is called *pakvamudgānna*, while the previously mentioned *pāyasa* is [referred to as] *kṛsara*.
Half [the weight] of milk, half that amount of jaggery and sugar-candy, mixed with half that amount of clarified butter.
In this very context, plantain fruit mixed with that rice-pudding—
thus, O Six-faced One, the fivefold food offering is proclaimed.
Half a *kulā* of mung beans and black gram, one *māḍhaka* of flat beans and chickpeas,
as well as king beans— all of these were entirely destroyed by them.
The kūṣmāṇḍa, panasa, lābu, kāliṅga, the two types of bṛhatī,
tripusa, karkarī, as well as satula,
vītuṣa, kadalī, kāravyāghrī, and likewise kṛtavedhuka.
Likewise, the root of a creeper, a bulbous root, and other roots endowed with firmness [should be used].
One fruit of the *prastha* measure is prescribed, whether it be slightly green or fully ripe;
one should cook it especially with whatever side-dishes (*vadaṃśa*) are available.
One should cook each of these preparations separately: all the aforementioned items, along with *marīca*, salt, clarified butter, cumin, and the juice of *ābala*.
One should properly mix *kulastha* powder, *siddhārtha*, black pepper, and cumin,
along with sugar, salt, water, and buttermilk.
When the soup has been cooked in this manner, one should add plantain and jackfruit;

it is said that sixty-four varieties of offerings, including cow's ghee, are to be presented. A portion of *kulmāṣa* (half-cooked grain) should be one-sixteenth part, while curd is said to be one-eighth part.
One should imagine that the portion of the *vasu* is called "well-cooked" (*sūpa*).
At the conclusion of the cooking, having cleansed the ground outside with a broom,
one should sprinkle it with pure water while accompanied by the sounding of umbrellas, conchs, and other instruments.
Then, one should cause everything to rise by means of the mantra "Huṃ.
Likewise, at the time of raising the food offering (naivedya), men should likewise suspend it.

The destruction of the crops is declared to be *nirmālya*; that substance having been avoided, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times. (Fifth line) Having again offered cooked food, one should then perform a hundred oblations with the *aghora-astra* mantra.
One should gradually place [the deities] upon the mandala in the southern part of the pavilion.
In this manner, according to the prescribed characteristics, one should fill the vessel with food;
one should provide boiled rice along with curd and condiments, and sprinkle it with ghee.
A wise person should make the vessel out of gold, silver, copper, or even a plantain leaf, or from pure bell-metal.
Above three-quarters [of its height], one should place a small cooking pot (sthālikā) in due order.
One should fill the vessel with food possessing the proper characteristics.
Having divided the sacrificial oblation into four parts, one should offer one portion,
accompanied by side dishes and combined with clarified butter.
It was filled with plantains, jackfruit, and mangoes, all bearing ripe fruit;
it was provided with sugar, curd, and cooked milk-rice (pāyasa).
Combined with ginger, one should offer it with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
with one portion alone, there shall be the offering for the retinue.
One [portion] is for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), while the remainder of the vessel is for the leftovers.
The remainder of that is proclaimed for the food of the attendants.
One should especially offer it in the shape of fire even to women;
if, out of delusion, one should enter that [residue] into a village, it will certainly destroy it.

The obligatory [rite] has been fully explained; now hear concerning the optional and the occasional. Having first performed the purification of the ground, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the heart-mantra.
Having properly strewn the ground, one should cover it with a cloth;
upon that, one should spread a plantain leaf with its tip pointing eastward and its end toward the north.
One should especially spread [offerings] over it and sprinkle them with clarified butter.
Having divided the sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) into three parts, one should offer two portions.
One portion shall remain as the residue for the vessels; furthermore, one should take an abundance of side dishes, clarified butter, threads, curd, betel-leaf, and other items.
The preceptor, endowed with the Astra-mudrā, should cause the Astra-mantra of the one who has sown the seeds of the quarters to be offered to the God of gods by means of the Hṛdaya-mantra. (Verse 8)
Having offered food, drink, as well as items to be sucked and licked with devotion, and having applied ointment to his hands, one should provide water for sipping.
Listen now to the procedure for food offerings and the procedure for drinking water.
One should fill clean vessels made of new copper or clay with water.
Water from a river, a lake, or a well is considered the best kind of water.
It should be well-cooled, strained through a cloth, and seasoned with cardamom and other spices.
One should cause the water to be offered according to this procedure with the heart-mantra;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should present it to Caṇḍeśa.
The measurement for the two pillars is proclaimed as the *balidāna*;
one should cause it to be offered to Nandīśa on the right side of the door.
(Line 4) On the left side of the door, however, one should cause it to be offered to Mahākāla.
Then one should offer [the bull] to Vṛṣabha in front of the fire;
likewise, to the host of Mothers in the south, and again to Nirṛti;
to Skanda in the western quarter, and to Jyeṣṭhā in the region of Vāyu.
To Durgā in the northwestern direction, and to Bhāskara in the northeast;
thereafter, one should especially offer a bali-oblation upon the pedestal situated in front.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, gandharvas, kinnaras,
pitṛs, dānavas, and nāgas— beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna and Antaka—
[one should worship them] with their own names placed in the middle, preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending in the dative case.
One should apply the instruction for the bali offering as "svāhāya" and "to all [beings]."
Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), together with mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa)—
[namely] camphor and powdered small sugar-candy— (line 8).

The wise one should take equal portions of the powder of the three fruits and employ it; at the end of the meal, he should offer this mouth-freshener, which is dear to Śiva. He should cause betel leaf to be offered to Śambhu along with one *prastha* of each fruit.
Four times as much leaf as fruit, together with the tongue and devoid of the stalk;
combined with the powder of *brahma* and provided with the fruit of the betel nut (*kramuka*);
that [leaf] broken and mixed with oil should be offered to Śiva.
The wise one should always cause this to be performed;
he should offer the sacrificial oblation to Cala, Caṇḍa, and to all [the deities].
Whatever has been offered to the Liṅga is known as *nirmālya*;
one should discard it upon the ground, into fire, or into water, or give it to herds of cows.
Because it is a binding impurity of the body, one should not consume *nirmālya*.
But if that which was eaten was done through negligence, one should perform the Atikṛcchra penance.
If one should transgress [this rule] through negligence, a wise person should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
upon touching [it], however, one should wash both hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should sprinkle all the images with pure water using the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as the floral offerings and the food offerings.
The food of the attendants and others is not to be eaten;
however, the food of Gaṇeśa is said to be edible for everyone.
That which is offered to the commander-in-chief is edible, for it increases one's vitality.
That which is unfit for consumption by devotees of Bhānu is fit to be offered to Bhāskara.
O Ravi, food and offerings for all others as well—this offering is indeed a great delusion; it is merely food that increases one's progeny.
The food offering of Madana is not to be eaten by Brahmins;
however, that which is offered to the goddess Umā is indeed fit to be eaten by everyone.
That which is offered to Hari is indeed the foremost among all things;
it is the food for Brahmins, and for the one who offers it to Brahmins, it is the very essence of Brahman. What is offered to the guardians of the world always brings about health and prosperity.
That which is an offering to Manmatha is said to be edible for all.
Now hear concerning the Prājāpatya and other penances as the occasion for atonement:
one should fast for a day in the morning and then conquer the mantra immediately thereafter.

I shall not eat in the evening; thereafter, one should mutter the Vāma-mantra. One should mutter the fifth [mantra] for three days, and the ninth and so forth for the first [period]. (Fourth line) Furthermore, one should not eat for three days, and especially beyond that.
Then, having meditated upon Sadāśiva, one should thereafter conquer the mantra of the faces.
One should recite it a thousand times every single day;
this is to be known as the Prājāpatya rite, which cuts away all sins.
One should eat only as much as fits into the hollow of one's hand for nine days; thus one conquers Guhyaka.

For five days, however, one should not eat at all, and one should recite the *Hṛdaya* mantra a thousand times. This is declared to be the *Atikṛcchra* penance; thereafter, one should perform the recitation every day.
The sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed by this very act. The Prājāpatya and other penances have been declared; now hear the procedure for the perpetual fire.
The most excellent preceptor should establish the fire in the south-eastern direction according to the prescribed rite.
Either square or circular, provided with three girdles,
and one cubit in width— this is said to be the measurement of the pit.

In the west or the south, one should place the fire in a pit shaped like a vulva or like an aśvattha leaf; one must protect it from being extinguished. One should worship the fire well with the root-offerings for as long as they last.
One should worship that which resides in the liṅga there, and offer oblations of clarified butter to that which resides in the fire.
The preceptor should worship the fire three times a day or once a day;
therein, the sequence consists of purification, sweeping, and the smearing with cow dung.
One should especially purify [it] with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
one should worship the fire with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.

One should strew *darbha* grass around [the fire] and then perform the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣeka*). Having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer the *Vyāhṛtis* in their proper sequence. (Verse 5) Having offered with the *Praṇava* mantra alone, there shall be sixteen [offerings].
Having offered the *caru*, at the conclusion of that, the *vyāhṛtis* are indeed offered.
Then, having offered the limbs of Brahmā, one should cause the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering to be performed.
One should perform the *brahmakūrca* rite with the *praṇītā* water and fuel sticks.
Listen now to the procedure for the perpetual fire and the characteristics of the mudrās;
it brings joy to the gods and likewise puts the asuras to flight.
Because of their gladdening and melting, this is the *mudrā* [of joy]...
[the *liṅga-mudrā*, the *namaḥ-kārā*, the one called *tāla*, and the *śaṅkha-mudrikā*].
Also the *surabhi-mukulī*, as well as the *āvāhī* and the *niṣṭhura*.
The one called Bīja, the Pañcamudrī, and that which consists of the divine [elements]; likewise, that called Sadāśiva by means of the Saṃhāramudrā;
and the Āsanīyā, Maheśā, and the ten mudrās beginning with Vajra.
The ṭaṅa-mudrā, the mahāmudrā, the one called ghaṇṭā, and the weapon-mudrā; (third line) ...-mudrā and the bow-mudrā—these thirty-two are proclaimed.
Known as the Liṅgamudrā, one should display it with the [thumb] severed;
having placed it in the region of the heart, it is called by means of a salutation.
One should shake [the hands] there with the two hands and form the mudrā known as Kharādhanā;
indeed, this is called the Śaṅkha-mudrā, which one should employ at the time of bathing.
Having performed the mudrā known as āvāhanī, one should likewise perform the invocation; then, specifically at the time of confinement, one should perform the mudrā known as saṃnidhā.
Likewise, in the visualization of power, one should display the primary seed-syllable as the principal [form].
One should also display the five-faced mudrā in the ritual of the faces. (6th line) ...In the absence of those substances, one should display [this] instead.
At the time of the installation of the one called Śiva, he should show [the disciple] in the presence of the deity.
Having formed the fist and raised it upward, with the two hands joined at the heart, this is called the *āsana* [mudrā];
likewise, one should display it while seated.
One should display the *tālamudrā* for the images of those of great renown (*maheśākhya*).
One should visualize the ten mudrās, beginning with the *vajra*, upon the ten hands. (Line 8) The *ṭaṅkamudrā* shall be their great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*), with [the fingers] slightly contracted.
The bow mudrā of these [deities] brings about the destruction of all enemies.
The sequence of mudrās has been fully explained according to their respective pairs;
[it includes] the mudrās for libation and the añjali, as well as the placement of hands upon the body and the ritual protection.
The offering of water for the feet, water for sipping, the food offering, the principal consecration, garments, ornaments, garlands, and other decorations are performed with both hands. (Second line:
The gifts, the rites of showing [the deity], and so forth, as well as the sprinkling, are performed while facing the deity.
The offering of water for the guest-rite (arghya) with joined palms, the libation (tarpaṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and so forth.
The wise practitioner should perform [the rite] according to the rules with both hands facing each other;
likewise, there should be sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the substances, deities, and mantras, as well as the sky.
With the hand turned downwards, one should likewise cover the limbs;

one should arrange the bed, the seat, the resolve, and the placing [of the vessel]. (4th line) One should also perform the sprinkling of the oblation and the offering of fragrance, flowers, and the arghya water.
The number of recitations for the consecration, as well as the additional offerings of bali oblations.
The consecration with ashes using the *trayambaka* mantra is performed by those two [hands] joined together,
employing all three— the middle, ring, and thumb fingers.

One should place the substances, deities, and mantras, and cause the offering of perfumes and other articles; one should sprinkle with the two *jyā* [straps] according to the rule. Having taken up the sprinkling from above, one performs the sprinkling from below.

With three applications of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) mixed with water and *kuśa* grass accompanied by the name-mantras— whatever has not been explicitly stated here for this deity, as spoken in the Śiva scriptures,
should be performed by the most excellent of teachers after observing the manual application of the hands.
