O Ṣaṇmukha, listen as I shall describe the complete method of propitiation in brief:
it is threefold, namely *cala*, *acala*, and *acalācala*.
A mountain made of metal should be known as mobile; a mountain made of stone is traditionally held to be both mobile and immobile.
A mountain made of clay should be known as immobile, as should those made of plaster, murals, or cloth-paintings.
[Just as with] a clay [mountain], so it is with one adorned with paintings, or a mural on a wall, or a painting on cloth.
Among them, one should worship the gods with food, clothing, and ornaments.
(………………………) by means of all such services; (second line:
[this applies] to that which is on a cloth, a mural painting, or a stone inlaid with pictures.
One should especially worship the ritual image along with the iconic image;
or, having fashioned the ritual image from clay, one may perform the worship of the gemstone image upon a pedestal.

Whether reaching down to the knees or up to the navel, according to the specific ritual procedure; in the case of a stone image devoid of painting, one should perform the dismissal of the deity after the installation of the metal linga.

For one whose ritual worship has been performed as prescribed and whose worship with the prescribed mantras has been completed, one should first perform the worship there and then cause the ritual worship to be carried out. (4th line) Or else, with devotion, there is sprinkling; or [the rite is performed] unmanifestly in the case of metalwork.
It is established alone, yet accompanied by its retinue and other such elements.
There, the sequence of worship should be performed with all ritual offerings;
furthermore, the images should be specially installed immediately thereafter.
The wise one should perform the oblation with sacrificial offerings, excluding the retinue and other such elements;
then, having performed the purification of the image according to the specific form of that image.
Then, having removed the garlands worshipped during the morning twilight with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
the wise practitioner should purify the earthen image— or likewise the *vicitrāsa*— with the *mukhapiṇḍa* and the breath,
or with *kuśa* grass.
If, however, that mountain described in such a manner consists solely of water;
Gold is purified by night-soil, silver by salt;
copper is purified by sour gruel, and bronze is purified by ash.
Then, having bathed the bronze images on every festival day,
the preceptor, having placed a flower upon the head, should fashion two faces;
he should also assign Dharma and the other [deities] to the corners and prepare the water for washing the feet.
And one should sequentially place adharma and the others upon the mouth and the other [limbs] as false.
Having first honored [the deity] with the three qualities, one should worship Hari in the center;
in that middle space, having placed the ritual action, [one should draw] an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
In the center of that, one should install the deity consisting of thirty-eight kalās;
then, one may commence either the ritual worship or the image-worship according to the specific rite intended.
One should cause the deity to enter with the Sadyojāta mantra, but install him with the Guhyaka mantra.
But complete cessation is accomplished by Aghora, while presence is attained by Tatpuruṣa.
One should offer the arghya water upon the head with the heart-mantra;
likewise, one should cause the pādya, ācamana, and arghya to be given with the heart-mantra.
One should perform the consecration with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
the wise one should sprinkle [the disciple] with water from the *aghora* mantra while reciting the *kuśa*-mantra without attachment.
Garments, ornaments, the sacred thread, and a mirror should be offered with the Īśāna mantra;
one should cause the water for the feet (pādya) to be given with the Sadyojāta mantra.
(Line 6) One should offer a garland upon the head with the [mantra of] Tatpuruṣa, and incense with the [mantra of] Tatpuruṣa as well.
One should indeed worship Dīpa with the Netra-mantra and Gaurī with the Vāma-mantra. One should install Gaṅgā in the eastern quarter, Vināyaka in the south,
and Senāpati at the side, [and others] in the corners in due order.
One should present the food offering with the mantra "devasya tvā";
having given the water for sipping (ācamana) with the heart-mantra, one should then dismiss the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
The wise one should cause betel-leaf to be offered for the purpose of perfuming the mouth.
This is declared to be the propitiation of all [deities]. Now hear concerning the seer (*ṛṣi*) beginning with the *praṇava*.
Oṃ; its seer is said to be Brahmā and others.
The goddess is Chandodevī, and the deity is the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
For the Sadyojāta mantra, the presiding deity is Brahmabhakta;
Gāyatrī is said to be the meter, and Gautama is the seer (ṛṣi).
Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the Vāmadeva mantra;
its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and likewise, its seers are the Ātreyas.
Rudra, in the form of the Aghora weapon, is its presiding deity;
likewise, Viśvāmitra is the seer, conjoined with the Triṣṭubh metre.
(Line 4) Maheśa is the presiding deity of the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
The Bṛhatī meter is said [to belong] to the Ṛṣi (……), together with Cala.
The form of the mantra is Īśāna, and Śiva is the presiding deity therein;
it is joined with the Jagatī meter, and Bhāradvāja is likewise the seer (ṛṣi).
Thus, the form known as Sādākhyamūrti consists of the five Brahmans;
now hear the procedure for the perpetual festival according to the specific [tradition] of Aṭṭālabhaṭṭāraka.
The *vākuta* [pedestal] made of gilded gold and copper, together with the hands and elbows, was forgotten.
It is held at the height of a palm-tree (*tāla*), provided with a pericarp (*karṇikā*), along with the fingers and the rise, and then with eight pericarps.
(7th line) Thus, one should place the vessel within the northern part of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*).
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, one should offer flowers, food, and water for honor (arghya).
The "lesser" (kanyasa) [form] is described as being extensive and performed twice daily with the fire-linga;
however, that which involves the arghya-linga is celebrated as the "middling" (madhyama).
The *liṅga* made of *canna* wood is proclaimed to be the most excellent;
its height is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and its width is said to be double that.
The tip [of the linga] should be five finger-breadths wide, and it should be adorned everywhere with perfumes and garlands;
having thus worshipped that linga, one should likewise worship the Raudra and Pāśupata [mantras].
Four-armed and three-eyed, blazing at the peak of his crest,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and possessed of a fierce appearance to behold;
holding the tip of the trident-shaft with his left hand, which was adorned with bracelets.
The trident, at the base of its staff, is held with the fist of the right hand.
The fist should be facing downwards, while the bracelet is turned upwards;
in the right [hand] there is a rosary, and with the left hand he holds a noose.
Having assumed the symmetrical standing posture (*samabhaṅgasthānaka*) according to the previously mentioned measurements,
the wise artisan should likewise fashion the King of Weapons (*Astrarāja*).

One should invoke the deity with the *sadyojāta* mantra; the installation (*sthāpana*) should be performed with the *vāmadeva* mantra; proximity (*sānnidhya*) is established with the *aghora* mantra; and one should worship with the *puruṣa* mantra. (Sixth line) One should likewise display the weapon-mudrā (*astramudrā*) as well as the mudrā known as salutation (*namaskāra*).
One should worship that fierce Lord, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, for the sake of seeing [him].
[One should worship] the God standing with straight limbs, joined with a black axe,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Wearing the earth, its islands, and its oceans as his garment, with a gentle gaze and a smiling face,
he is the embodiment of the moon-crested Lord, or likewise the embodiment of the weapon.

One should worship either an image-form or another [form] in a *liṅga*. …… [In the second line: …… and when the fierce wind has subsided, one should perform the worship of the King of Weapons alone, established within the *liṅga*.
And with the Pāśupata weapon-mantra, one should offer oblations eight hundred times with the heart-mantra.
Having summoned his two attendants, he [provided them] with turbans and upper garments;
they were endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
All [the priests], with sacred grass in their hands and adorned with perfumes and garlands,
should place the liṅga and especially the image upon the heads of those two.
It should be provided with a canopy, a parasol, and joined with peacock feathers and chowries.
Equipped with all kinds of musical instruments and attended by devotees of various sects,

[one should perform worship] three times— circumambulating [the deity] clockwise: for the gratification of Brahmā in the forenoon, for the form of Śiva at midday, and for the gratification of Viṣṇu at night.
One should lead [the deity] above and in front, and likewise at its end;
having first performed a circumambulation accompanied by the *bhṛṅgiṇī* rhythm and *tāla*.
One should then perform the second circumambulation of the attendants;
[the dance for] the bull is the vṛṣatāla, and likewise the Āgneyī and Bhṛṅgiṇī.
For the Mothers, the musical instrument is the *jhallarī*; for Vighneśa, it is the *ṭaṅkiri*.
For Ṣaṇmukha, it is the water-pot (*ghaṭa*); and for Jyeṣṭhā, it is the *kuñcitālaka*. On the banks, embankments, and forts, [one should worship] Durgā; and on uneven ground, Caṇḍikā.
Gāndhāra, Sampūrṇakaulya, Tāma, Andhāvaṇa, and Kauśika.
Accompanied by Bhṛṅgī, Pañcama, and Mallatāla, it is the glorious Kāmara and Saumara;
joined with Takkeśī and Balitāla, he who is great in the sequence of Yakṣa, Kara, and Āga.
At the city gate, with the sound of musical instruments and accompanied by the blast of conchs,
he should then circumambulate three times the throne situated within the city.
The abode resorted to by all the gods, especially the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha),
is the grand display of the offering (baliḍambaram) for the sake of the strength of the three worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar.
It belongs to the divine sages, to human beings, and especially to all things moving and stationary.
When it has arisen for all beings, it is called Bali because it bestows strength.
For the purpose of circumambulating the three worlds, one performs the circumambulation of the abode of Śiva:
first is the circumambulation of Bhūḥ, and second is the circumambulation of Bhuvaḥ.

The third circumambulation is toward the heavens, indeed the circumambulation of great power; Śiva is the auspicious world for the protection of the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven. (Sixth line) He is the abode of all the gods and is remembered as the Mūlādhāra.
He circumambulated Śambhu, the cause of the protection of the world.
It is to be constantly served for the sake of Śiva by the gods, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and the lords of sages, as well as by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.

Then, one should resort to the great sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*) of the deities and their consorts during the times of the circumambulation of the offerings and during the worship of the retinue.
Having performed a circumambulation here, one should avoid crossing its shadow;
then, having entered the interior of Śabarī’s sacrificial altar,
there shall be a fire-enclosure equal in measure to that of Indra.
To the south of Yama is the Bhṛṅgiṇītāla, and in the southwest is the Marmatālaka.
In the western quarter there is Navatāla, while in the north-western quarter is Balitālaka; (in the second line:
Kauśikī is said to be in the northern quarter, and likewise Ṭaṅkirī is in the north-eastern quarter.
The *baliliṅga* should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned procedure;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should enter the temple.
Taking your stand at the doorway, perform the washing of the feet;
[offer] sandals, the deity Vṛṣa, and all the ritual services on every side.
Having worshipped the bull with water for the feet and other offerings while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra,
the preceptor should first enter the temple and then place [the bull] in its proper place.
Taking the deity from the *liṅga*, he should install him within the image.

Then, one should cause the fierce blow to be struck with the fierce mantra. Then, hearing the sound of the *bali* offering, the *piśācas* and *brahmarākṣasas* go outside the village, bestowing abundance of wealth and grain.
Having thus performed the perpetual festival, the characteristics of recitation (japa) are described:
O fair-faced one, for each individual count of the recitation, [one should use] a finger.
One should know that a lamp with a painted wick (*rekhā*) has eight times the merit; one with a son as the wick (*putradīpa*) has ten times;
one with a conch-shell has a hundred times; one with coral (*pravāla*) has a thousand times;
one with crystal (*sphaṭika*) has ten thousand times; and one with pearls (*mauktika*) is said to have a hundred thousand times the merit.
With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [are said to be the count]; with gold beads, one crore is declared.
By men constantly reciting [the mantra] ten crores of times using *kuśa*-grass knots, or indeed by the recitation of auspicious *rudrākṣa* beads, the fruit is multiplied infinitely.
One should know that the Rudrākṣa is indeed the recitation; there is no counting of the recitation. When joined with recitation, it is meditative absorption; thereafter is the hymn and the mantra.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Pañcabrahma*, the *Śivāṅgas*, the *Vyomavyāpin*, and the *Tryambaka* mantras according to one's capacity, while circumambulating three times. According to the authority stated by Bharata, one should likewise perform the *Tāṇḍava* dance and the singing.
The añjali gesture consists of the right hand being bent at four finger-breadths.
Having taken the flower-water, the wise one should place it without finishing;
this is declared to be "cupful water" (culukodaka), [offered] from the feet up to oneself.
The bath should last for two *ghaṭikās*, and the *atināma* [offering] for one *ghaṭikā*.

The presentation of food (*nivedya*) should last for half a *ghaṭikā*, while the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) is equal to that. (Line 5) The daily fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) lasts for half a [period], and the daily festival (*nityotsava*) lasts for two *nāḍikās*.
The single channel of the Tāṇḍava should be well-practiced at every junction (saṃdhyā).
Starting from sunrise until ten nāḍikās have passed,
that period is called "morning" (prātaḥkāla) and is also termed "forenoon" (pūrvāhna).
Beginning from the end of the forenoon (pūrvāhna), the period lasting for ten nāḍikās should be known as midday (madhyāhna);
thereafter, the afternoon (aparāhna) is described.
Beginning from the end of midday, [the period] lasting for ten nāḍikās...
It should be known as the afternoon; then the time of evening is described.

Starting from sunset, seven and a half *nāḍikās* are renowned as *pradoṣa*; listen now to the [period of] half a watch (*ardhayāma*) following that. Starting from the end of *pradoṣa*, it consists of three *nāḍikās* plus one-third [of a *nāḍikā*].
Half a watch is thus declared; now midnight is described:
it begins from that [half-watch] and lasts for ten nāḍīs.
That which is known as midnight is also called the end of the night;
it consists of three nāḍīs, or three quarters of an hour, prior to the rising of the sun.
Having understood that this is declared to be the end of the night, one should perform all [rituals] accordingly.

The collection of water, the gathering of flowers, and likewise the performance of worship must be done at sunrise, or one may collect the water at the end of the night. One should perform the installation of the deities and the ritual bathing at the time of dawn.
Starting from the time of dawn until the Kāśika nāḍikā.
O Prajāpati, the rites for the sacred site should be performed for that duration;
first, however, comes the consecration of the festival, preceded by the ritual sowing of sprouts.
In the evening, the wise one should begin the binding of the protective thread (rakṣāsūtra),
as well as during the installation, the sprinkling with water, and likewise during the laying of the foundation (garbhanyāsa).
One should perform all the ritual offerings (*adhivāsana*) at midnight;
specifically, during the final part of the night, for the purpose of pleasing all the deities. At that time, one should produce the five great sounds (*pañcamahāśabda*) to avert inauspiciousness.
In the shrine of the western door, however, there is a slight difference in the worship of Śiva:
one should worship Nandīśa and Narmadā on the right side of the door,
and Vijayā and Sindhu on the left side of the door.
One should visualize the gatekeepers, beginning with Nandin, as before;
having worshipped the bull in the west, one should worship Skanda in the east.
One should worship the retinue there, beginning with Vṛṣa and ending with Vighneśvara;
one should offer all the ritual services (upacāras) while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra.
(Second line) One should arrange the seat, the coverings, and so forth, as previously described.
Thus, Śiva is worshipped at the twilight for the sake of oneself and for the sake of others;
listen now to the meritorious fruit of the worship performed by one who is unable [to perform it himself]:
it is auspicious, brings fame, increases longevity, and increases nourishment.
The Adṛṣṭa [Purāṇa] bestows liberation and grants the fruits of all gifts and sacrifices;
by rescuing seven generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
What name can be given by people to Śiva, who is perfectly complete?
Whatever is done for the devotees of Śiva is done for Śiva himself. (5th line) [Thus in the Vātula Tantra, in the Saṃhitā of a thousand verses]
The chapter on daily worship is completed.
Salutations to Śrī Mīnākṣī Sundareśa. Oṃ, salutations to the venerable Guru. (Sixth line: Salutations to Guha. Salutations to the goddess Śrī Sarasvatī. In the month of Plavaṅga... (etc.)
(…) at Itnāpatinattil, [this is] the Vātulāgama;
copied by the hand of Ayyāsāmi Gurukkal, grandson of Kānāvūr [Gurukkal] and son of Cidambara Gurukkal and Ṣaṇmukha Gurukkal.
May there be auspiciousness! One who wields the bow and arrows should plant snow-mountain, camphor, bilva, sandalwood, peacock, elephant, and horse.
Having gone to the forest outside the village, let him proceed quickly;
within the forest, amidst the radiance, he should gradually place [the offerings] for his diversion:
coconut water combined with the essence of milk.
One should especially offer betel-leaf as an oblation.
He who takes up the Kirāta while observing the deer-hunt—
some should perform the sequence of combat, while some should stand ready for battle.
Then, having entered that hall equipped with all kinds of musical instruments,
the six-faced goddess [Pārvatī] took special delight in it during that night.
One should especially adorn the God of gods with ornaments and other such items;

having bathed him according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship him with particular care. (Fifth line) In the center of the assembly hall, one should gradually tie the marriage-thread (kautuka).
One should perform a circumambulation of the village accompanied by all musical instruments.
Having reached the assembly pavilion, the ceremonial bathing should take place as before.
And on the ninth day, the procedure for the fragrance festival shall be performed.
On a pure, level ground, having placed a vessel upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should apply black fragrant paste and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as before.
Having performed a circumambulation of the palace and entered the assembly pavilion,
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made and then sprinkle [the area] with pure water. Then,
one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), and the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
Then one should worship Kumāra, beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti.
The wise should then perform the deposition of the thirty-eight kalās, starting from the crown (makuṭa) and so forth in sequence,
and offer incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, as well as water for the feet and water for sipping.
Having gazed at the prince for a moment, the astrologer should perform the sacrifice;
he should then offer fragrant oil and smear him with yakṣakardama paste.
Having smeared Skandadeva with a pigment made from the fruit of the Jambu tree,
and having worshipped him as previously described, together with the two Śaktis,
one should apply [the pigment] to the region of the goddess's neck and between her breasts.
One should offer the root-fragrance, and thereafter the fragrance of the Lord of the Sacrifice (Yageśvara).
Thereafter, at the conclusion of that [rite], one should cause the teacher to receive his portion;
at the conclusion of that, the king should cause it to be given, and he should cause it to be given to all the castes.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with jewel garlands and the like,
one should especially decorate the God together with Gaurī.
One should worship and cause [another] to worship the cloth-painting (paṭa) endowed with the Puṣpaprabhā [mantra];
having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should then cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented.
Afterward, one should cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla), provided with mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa), to be given.
Having removed the cloth, one should offer incense, lamps, and other offerings to the Lord of Gods;
then, one should gradually place the *pavitra* (sacred thread) together with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having paid homage to the Lord of Gods, one should inform him of the festival;
[offering] the turban, the upper garment, and all the ornaments. (8th line) Holding the vessel of *arghya* in hand, and likewise standing upon that pedestal.
Reciting the mantra of Skanda, he joined it with the left side.
Holding the left footstool with both hands,
she took hold of the Lord of Gods, who was seated in the palanquin and served by all the deities.

There were kettledrums and maddala drums, as well as flutes and lutes; it was provided with various musical instruments and adorned with various banners. (Second line) It was accompanied by the ghaṭa drum, and the musicians there played the mṛdaṅga drums, O Lord.
Accompanied by songs and dances, [he performed] in the presence of the God of gods.
Again and again, he should utter a harsh, discordant sound;
having performed a circumambulation of the palace, he should likewise go outside to the seventh house.
Having shown himself to the people, he should then enter the pavilion for the performance and cause entertainment to be provided,
accompanied by dance and song. (4th line) Having established the prince there, he should honor him with camphor and other such offerings.
One should worship with jasmine flowers, garlands, and all kinds of fragrances.
Having worshipped with pearl garlands and other offerings, the best of preceptors should perform the sacrifice;
thereafter, he should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and cause incense, lamps, and so forth to be offered.
One should place [the image] upon a chariot or a palanquin at the moment of success;
a procession should be organized, proceeding slowly along each row.
Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas, joined with the sound of hymns,
accompanied by the noise of musical instruments, and joined with song and dance.
Then one should place the youth in the assembly hall;
subsequently, after removing [the obstacles] with dance, instrumental music, and so forth during the night,
one should perform the auspicious bath (*kautuka-snāna*) prior to the break of dawn.
And it should be beautifully adorned, like a riverbank or a lake.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should prepare nine new pitchers;
one should worship the nine holy sites (*tīrtha*), such as the Gaṅgā and others, with their respective mantras.
Having worshipped Mahāśakti and performed the thousand-fold ablution,
the preceptor then enters the temple and adorns it;
O Six-faced One, this is especially so at the time of dawn.
The preceptor should place the boy upon a chariot or a palanquin.
Having performed a complete circumambulation of the village and entered the pavilion of the assembly hall,
one should cause all musical instruments to resound in the area in front of the deity.
In the presence of the deity, one should especially perform the consecration of the site (*sthala-siddhi*),
along with the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful oblation (*arghya*), accompanied by incense and lamps.
The most excellent preceptors (*deśikottama*) should cause all these ritual services (*upacāra*) to be presented.
Having offered to the God all the cakes, cooked rice, and side dishes, one should especially offer water for drinking;
thereafter, one should give water for sipping (ācamana) and betel leaf as a mouth-freshener.
Then one should worship the Youth (Kumāra), endowed with incense and lamps;
the procedure is to apply cow-dung [as an offering] in the center in front of the God.
Having prepared two sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila), one should cover them with darbha grass and flowers;
having worshipped them with the Hṛdaya mantra, they should be beautified with auspicious sprouts. (Line 7) Having placed the mortar upon the pestle, one should present the sacrificial mound.
And having placed the Śakti in the western position, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Ghee for the offering on the head, oil, sacrificial dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains;
likewise, one droṇa or half a droṇa of dried turmeric.
Having placed [the substance] there upon the mortar and ground it gradually,
the wise one should then place the great spear upon the sacrificial mound.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using the Śakti-mantra, the preceptors, having struck the eastern drum, should perform the powder festival. Then, the preceptors,
using the Vyomavyāpin mantra, should trample the ground.
It was filled with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and crowded with singing and instrumental music.
Then, the devotees should perform the powder festival;
having collected that powder, they should worship the Six-faced One with the heart-mantra.
Then, with this Kumāra-mantra, one should cause betel to be given;
likewise, having performed the anointing with dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains, one should cause the powder to be given.
Then the preceptor should sequentially install the deities and Śakti in the [mandala],
and he should cause the king’s devotees to be provided with oil and flour-meal.
Having quickly performed a circumambulation and given the powder to the people of the village,

one should then enter the house and perform a ritual bath at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). (Line 7) Furthermore, the collection of water from the sacred fords must be performed according to the prescribed rules.
One should place nine pitchers, and in the very center, Manonmanī; likewise, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, Sarasvatī,
Sindhu, Godāvarī, and Kāverī, in their proper order.
One should worship [the deities] with their respective mantras from the east up to the northeast.
[This should be done] at the shore of a lake, a river, or likewise in a pond.
Having adorned the bank and constructed a beautiful water-shed (prapā),
one should worship two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) with the Praṇava.
Having placed the Śakti to the west, one should set down the jars (kalaśas) to its east.
Having taken the perforated jars, one should wrap them with thread;
(4th line) having filled them with water from sacred fords, one should place them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
thereafter, the performer, according to the rules, should arrange the tufts of grass (kūrca). (5th line)
One should specifically place substances joined with auspicious sprouts;
the procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) has been declared, as well as the sequence for the procedure of the five earths (pañcamṛt).
One should worship all the deities of the directions in sequence with fragrant water,
having summoned all the sacred fords and the thirty-three gods.
Having summoned the eighteen classes [of attendants] and bathed them at the sacred ford,
the wise ones should then install the Root-Brahma-mantra, the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), and likewise the Mālā-mantra,
as well as this Kumāra-mantra, in the midst of the sacred ford.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should cause the Śakti to immerse herself in the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Whatever thousand-fold bath one performs there brings about the destruction of all sins;
having entered that sacred ford, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having bathed that amulet, one should then worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
thereafter, having entered the palace, one should provide all kinds of musical instruments.
One should perform the ritual of sacrifice and worship for the forms of the deities at the conclusion of the fire oblation;
specifically, one should bathe the primary image according to the prescribed sequence.
One should bathe the principal image with the water from the jars situated on the sacrificial altar,

worship it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, and present the great oblation (*mahāhavis*). (Verse 4) Having offered the ritual food (*bali*), one should conclude the rite at the *balipīṭha* in the prescribed sequence.
At the conclusion of the offering, one should have musical instruments sounded, accompanied by lamps. (Fifth line:
All [the participants], maintaining silence, should dismiss the deities.
Having circumambulated the village, [one should place] the banner at the front of the pedestal.

Having entered and remained there as prescribed, one should perform the lowering of the flag to the accompaniment of the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments; then, one should sequentially have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited.
One should place the staff-base, the lotus, and the ball of rice;
then, having entered the inner sanctum, one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering.
Having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, one should worship well with eight flowers.
O Kauśika of virtuous conduct, listen as I describe the ritual for the worship of Sumitra,
which includes the bathing of Sumitreśa and is accompanied by garments and ornaments.
One should perform the fire-ritual as prescribed, accompanied by oblations beginning with *sumitrā*.
At the conclusion of the oblation, there should be an offering, and one should present betel leaf.
Having worshipped it especially with incense and lamps,
and having provided it with an image made of food along with an offering vessel;

Having taken up the Śaktis and the deities according to the sequence of dismissal and offerings, one should observe silence; then, having offered the supreme Śiva-portion, one should dismiss the deities of the offerings.
(Third line) One should likewise ensure the lamps are extinguished and announce the time for the meal.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should cast the bali offering upon the great seat (mahāpīṭha).
Having washed his feet, he should likewise enter the temple;
there, he should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
Thereafter, one should cause a sacrificial fee to be given, together with cows, land, and gold;
the lowest is said to be [one] niṣka, and the middle is ten niṣkas.
Twenty excellent niṣkas shall be the sacrificial fee for the Ācārya;
one-tenth of that, along with the fee, shall be for the Mūrtipās.
All the implements of the sacrifice should be presented to the Deśika.
He should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his capacity to the devotees and attendants;
he should feed the poor, the blind, other devotees, and the Brahmins;
and on the following day, he should indeed perform the festival of Gaurī.
O Kauśika of virtuous conduct, listen as I shall explain the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for Gaurī,
the sacrifice of power (*śaktiyāga*), and the sequence of events during the first watch of the night.
Beginning the festival at evening, [he should lead] the Kumāra [to the Śaktikā...];
having gone there,
he should immediately thereafter perform the circumambulation of the village and enter the assembly pavilion.
Following this, one should offer incense, lamps, and the waving of lights (nīrājana).
Then, having presented the great sacrificial oblation (mahāhavis), one should offer betel leaf.
Thus, accompanied by songs and dances, one should perform the royal honors (rājopacāra).
And this great festival brings happiness to all the world;
it is beneficial for all people, meritorious, and a source of prosperity for the entire kingdom.

There shall be the destruction of all poverty, the increase of victory for kings, and the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; thus is the festival described in sequence. (5th line) [Thus, in the *Kumāratantra*, in the inquiry of Kauśika, within the *Mahāsaṃhitā*...]
The thirteenth chapter: The Ritual for the Great Festival.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for expiation (*prāyaścitta*):
when the temple has fallen, been broken, cracked, or likewise become dilapidated.
When the doorposts and pillars are missing, when the surrounding retinue is deficient,
when the proportions of the images are lacking, and likewise when they are decayed or unstable.
At the time of circumambulating the village, on the day following the breaking of an image,
and during the times of offering oblations to the weapons— it falls down, indeed broken.
When there is a crow, a blue jay, or [other] impure substances in the vessel;
when the daily worship is neglected, or the daily festival is omitted; when the fire has been extinguished, the fire has decayed, or the offerings for the *bali* have been abandoned.
Upon touching a Caṇḍāla, or even upon touching one who has killed his master,
or upon touching one devoid of the sacred thread, one should touch another image;
likewise, it should be done when [the image] is devoid of fragrance or devoid of clothing.
And when there is no incense, nor even a lamp for the food offering.
When the water for washing the feet and the materials for the arghya offering are lacking; when the side-dishes are absent;
when betel is missing; and when the mouth-freshener is lacking.
At the time of the circumambulation of the sacrificial offering, if it should likewise be devoid of lamps,
and if an anthill or similar growth has arisen, the body is consumed by fire.
At the time of lifting the water-pot (*kalaśa*), if it should fall and break,
or if anything from the fan (*vyajana*) up to the moving objects, as well as the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) or its pillars,
should by negligence be consumed by fire or fall, [the following applies].
When the annual festival has been neglected, and when that which is intended for the festival has been omitted.
O Kauśika of noble vows, listen now to the penance that must be performed;
when [the fault] has arisen in this manner, the following expiation is prescribed.
When the palace has fallen or been destroyed, and furthermore when one's own [residence] is damaged,
the principal oblation must be performed with this mantra of Kumāra.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited according to the mantra for this youth,
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there at the conclusion; specifically,
when the image has fallen, one should begin the rejoining of the fracture.
One should fashion a substitute image for one that is worn out, broken, or shattered.

One should again place another [vessel], endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, during the rite of consecration; or else, one may install other jars in the same manner as before, following the prescribed sequence.
Having recited the Pañcabrahma mantra one hundred times, one should especially perform the installation;
if the pedestal is broken or worn out, one should prepare another pedestal.
(Line 4) One should [recite] the Pañcabrahma and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), and the Kumāra-mantra one thousand times.
Having likewise established the lotus-seat specifically in that same manner,
one should perform the re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) upon the hand, the mouth, and so forth;
and [one should likewise perform the re-consecration] upon the image, the artisan, the touch, and the re-consecration itself.
Having then performed the installation in eighty-one jars,
the wise one should lift up that image and recite the Kumāra-mantra one hundred times.
The re-establishment should be performed according to the path taught in the scriptures;
at that time, one should fashion an image of iron for the world-protectors when they are deficient by one digit (kalā).
One should fashion the head-parts as before;
that material should be fashioned from copper in the same proportions.
Furthermore, if the maker fashions it in another form, the patron perishes.
Therefore, with every effort, one should fashion that form. It may be made of clay, for it is perishable; then the trident is installed again.
At the base of the garland, with the six limbs, one should likewise install Kumāra and Brahmā.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times for each [deity], one should begin the re-installation;
having again prepared the variegated seat, one should sprinkle it in sequence as before.

On that day, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) and especially the ritual bathing (snapana); if [the rites] such as the pavitra have been interrupted, one should then arrange them as before.
...as far as those images were in the presence of [the teacher],
having specially installed them with the Mūla-brahman and the six ancillaries one thousand and eight times,
and likewise having performed the purification of the mantra.

One should perform nine hundred [recitations] during the consecration; therefore, do so. At the time of the festive procession, or even if the image should fall, one should especially sprinkle it after reciting the *brahmakūrca* mantra eight hundred times.
Then, having performed a peace-offering (śānti-homa) that cuts away all defects,
one should immediately recite the mantra a hundred times if the worship of even a single twilight prayer has been omitted.
One should perform double the worship there and always recite the *puṇyāha* formula;
at midday, if the worship has been omitted, one should recite the Vāma mantra one hundred times.
Then, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the jar with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances.
In the evening, when the ritual worship has been omitted, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times.
O Brahmins, one should perform the worship twice as much as before, following the sequence as previously described.

Likewise, at midnight, one should perform the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while [the mantra] is empty. Having recited the *Vyomatantra* ten times and having especially worshipped it, one should establish the Destroyer of Asuras (*asurāntaka*) for one day by means of the "empty" [mantra].
Having performed one hundred and eight recitations with the root-mantra and the six limbs,
and having dismissed [the deity] for three days, he should consecrate [the disciple] with the empty jars.

It is declared that through worship, [the deity] is to be propitiated for one month; likewise, there is a void for the Tatpuruṣa [face] according to the sequence of the hands. Having performed the ablution fifty times, it shall likewise be especially effective.
For two months of worship, one should perform the *śūnya* rite and recite the mantra of Īśa one hundred times;
for the bath, one should worship the Destroyer of Asuras with twenty-five [offerings].
For three months of worship, one should perform the *śūnya* rite and consecrate with nine jars.

Likewise, having performed the eightfold ablution (*aṣṭaka-snapana*), it shall bring about all-pervading peace. If [the fetus] is absent from the tenth month onwards, one should recite the *pañcabrahma* mantra a hundred times.
One should perform the sprinkling with water and the special feeding of Brahmins;
for a year and so forth, [the rite is] empty, and the eighth [rite] consists of the eightfold worship.

One should perform the sprinkling with water and offer the great oblation (*mahāhavis*). [This applies when] the worship of two-year-old [cows] is deficient; [then there must be] one hundred and eightfold worship, as well as the sprinkling with water and the thousand-fold recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
If the worship has been neglected for three years, there shall be a sprinkling with water;
having caused the Brahmins to recite the *puṇyāha* formula, one should then feed them. For a neglect of four years or more, one should perform a sprinkling ceremony (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
O Prince, he should recite this garland-mantra one hundred and eight times;
at its conclusion, he should perform a ritual bath there and have the fire-offering mantras for the directions performed.
Ten years of worship purify the void;
therein, after performing a thousand ablutions, special worship shall take place.
In a place devoid of daily festivals, one should install the Destroyer of Asuras;
and in a place devoid of daily ablutions, [one should install him] on the occasions of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti) and at the equinoxes (viṣuva).
Having recited the root mantra one hundred times, as well as this [mantra] for Kumāra—
On other days as well, one should perform the ritual bathing twice.
With unguents such as oily substances, fruits, flowers, and perfumes—
even when these are deficient— one shall conquer by means of a hundred root-mantra garlands.
If the sacrificial materials are lacking, there is a double penalty for those involved in the subsequent rite;
however, if the fire is extinguished, the villagers shall provide food for the sake of those who are hungry.
[Reciting] the root mantra eight hundred times...
having recited it one hundred times for the restoration of what is decayed, one should perform worship especially;
having performed the reconnection and having performed worship especially.
A wise person should perform the fire oblation especially every day.
If the *balikarma* is omitted, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times;
there, one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite and sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Upon being touched by a Caṇḍāla, one should discard all vessels and liquids;
having performed purification, one should sprinkle the house with purifying waters.
Having caused the *puṇyāha* to be recited, one should sprinkle [the child] with the *pavamāna* hymns.
One should say, "Purified, purified. Then this boy should mutter the *śatam*.
(4th line) After that, the bathing (*snapana*) should be performed, and likewise, one should give what has been prescribed.
But for one of another caste, if [the body] is touched, one should mutter the Mālā-mantra a hundred times.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra;
finally, having performed the oblation of the directions (*diśāhoma*) accompanied by all the ritual substances.
Then, having performed the ceremonial bathing according to the path prescribed in the scriptures,
if the image is touched by a Brāhmaṇa, it portends harm to the king and the kingdom.
If one should perform the worship out of delusion, one would obtain the kingdom and the realm;
then, having commenced the ritual as before, one should have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited.
(In the case of an image) produced specifically from anthills and the like, one should likewise proceed.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should fill [the vessel] with *vālīka* powder.
Then, having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should likewise perform the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*),
covering the image with a cloth while it is being heated by the fire.
If a temple, an image,
or likewise the surrounding walls are consumed by fire through negligence, one should cause the Diśāhoma sacrifice to be performed.
Thereafter, following the prescribed ritual, perform the ceremonial bathing;
and when the image has been consumed by fire, restore its form as it was before.
One should perform the re-consecration according to the path taught in the scriptures;
whatever has been mentioned or left unsaid, one should have it performed as part of the directional fire-offerings (*diśāhoma*).
Having presented the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), one should then offer betel leaf in due order.
Salutations to Guhā. Salutations to Śrī Mīnākṣī and Sundareśa. (In the 4th line:

In the year Plava, on the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the time of the Makara Saṃkrānti, [I received] the Vātulāgama from the preceptor Kāyavūr Cidambara Gurukkam Kumāra. (In the 5th line:)
May there be auspiciousness for the one who has been served by the six-faced [Kārttikeya] and the preceptor Śiva;
